challenges.title: The one God and the three Persons
challenges.summary: Distinguish nature from person, then test what the Creed actually protects.
challenges.source: OCA · The Holy Trinity

questions.prompt: What does the Nicene claim that the Son is of one essence with the Father deny?
choices: That the Father and Son are distinct Persons
That the Son is a creature of a different nature
That the Son became human
That God created the world
questions.explanation: The Nicene confession that the Son is of one essence with the Father denies that the Son is a creature of a different nature; it does not deny that Father and Son are distinct Persons.

questions.prompt: A friend says the Father, Son, and Spirit are simply three masks one Person wears. What is the problem?
choices: It divides the one divine nature
It denies the real distinction of the three Persons
It says God has no will
It makes the Son too human
questions.explanation: Three masks worn by one Person is modalism: it denies the real, eternal distinction of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: How many divine natures does Orthodox Trinitarian teaching confess?
choices: One
Two
Three
None
questions.explanation: Orthodox teaching confesses one divine nature, or essence, shared fully by the three Persons.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best avoids both tritheism and modalism?
choices: Three gods cooperate
One Person changes roles
Three distinct Persons share one divine nature
The Spirit is an impersonal power
questions.explanation: Three distinct Persons sharing one divine nature avoids both tritheism, which would make three gods, and modalism, which would make the Persons mere roles.

questions.prompt: Why does theology of the Trinity matter for Christian life?
choices: It replaces prayer with definitions
Communion with God is life in the Father through the Son in the Spirit
It proves humans become God by nature
It makes love optional
questions.explanation: Trinitarian doctrine matters because salvation and prayer are communion with the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit, not because definitions replace prayer.

challenges.title: Christ, the councils, and the Theotokos
challenges.summary: Work through the claims that Christ is truly God, truly man, and one Person.
challenges.source: OCA · Incarnation

questions.prompt: Why is the title Theotokos a Christological claim?
choices: Mary created the divine nature
The child born of Mary is the one divine Son in the flesh
Mary is a fourth Person of the Trinity
It denies Christ had a human body
questions.explanation: Theotokos is a claim about Jesus: the child born of Mary is personally the one divine Son in the flesh. It does not mean Mary created the divine nature.

questions.prompt: What did Chalcedon confess about Christ?
choices: Two persons with one will
One Person in two complete natures, divine and human
One mixed nature with no distinction
A human body with no human mind
questions.explanation: Chalcedon confessed one Person in two complete natures, divine and human, without confusion or division.

questions.prompt: If Christ lacked a human mind, what crucial affirmation would be lost?
choices: That he was truly and fully human
That God is one
That Mary was Jewish
That creation is good
questions.explanation: A complete human nature includes a human mind; without it, Christ would not be truly and fully human.

questions.prompt: Which text most directly states that the Word became flesh?
choices: John 1:14
Genesis 1:1
Psalm 23:1
Acts 17:28
questions.explanation: John 1:14 states directly that the Word became flesh.

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to call the Incarnation a temporary disguise?
choices: Because the Word ceased to be God
Because the Word truly assumed humanity
Because the Church denies divine transcendence
Because resurrection was metaphorical
questions.explanation: The Incarnation is not a temporary disguise because the Word truly assumed humanity and remains incarnate.

challenges.title: Icons, salvation, and holy life
challenges.summary: Connect visible worship to the Incarnation and salvation as participation in grace.
challenges.source: OCA · Church Art / Theosis

questions.prompt: What is the central theological reason Christ can be depicted in an icon?
choices: God has always had a human body
The eternal Word truly became visible in human flesh
Every image is automatically holy
Icons replace Scripture
questions.explanation: Christ can be depicted because the eternal Word truly became visible in human flesh; icons do not claim that God the Father has a body.

questions.prompt: In Orthodox teaching, theosis means…
choices: Becoming another god by nature
Sharing in God’s life by grace
Escaping the created world
Earning divinity through perfect behavior
questions.explanation: Theosis is sharing in God’s life by grace, not becoming God by nature or earning divinity.

questions.prompt: Why is “mere symbolism” an inadequate account of the Eucharist?
choices: Because Orthodox worship has no symbols
Because the Eucharist is genuine communion in Christ, not only mental recollection
Because bread is evil
Because only clergy receive communion
questions.explanation: For Orthodoxy the Eucharist is genuine communion in Christ, not only an act of mental recollection, though it uses signs and symbols.

questions.prompt: How are faith and works related in James 2?
choices: Works buy salvation
Faith is living and becomes visible in mercy
Works replace prayer
Faith never affects conduct
questions.explanation: James presents faith as living trust that becomes visible in mercy; works do not purchase salvation.

questions.prompt: What does Pascha centrally proclaim?
choices: The soul’s escape from matter
Christ’s actual resurrection and victory over death
Only a seasonal renewal of optimism
That suffering is unreal
questions.explanation: Pascha centrally proclaims Christ’s actual resurrection and victory over death.

challenges.title: Reasoning for the faith
challenges.summary: Respond carefully to objections, identify what a text supports, and avoid overclaiming.
challenges.source: OCA · Scripture & Tradition

questions.prompt: “The Trinity means one God is three gods.” Which reply first corrects the category mistake?
choices: The Church has no doctrine of God
One divine nature is confessed in three distinct Persons
Three gods are united in purpose
The Father alone is God
questions.explanation: The correction is categorical: Christians confess one divine nature in three distinct Persons, not three gods.

questions.prompt: “Calling Mary Theotokos makes her the origin of God.” What is the strongest correction?
choices: The title speaks of the identity of her Son, not the origin of divinity
Mary is eternal
The Incarnation never happened
The title only means a moral teacher was born
questions.explanation: Theotokos speaks of the identity of Mary’s Son, not of Mary as the origin of divinity.

questions.prompt: “Icons are automatically idols.” What distinction should a careful response examine?
choices: Whether art is old enough
Whether an image is venerated as a witness or worshipped as a god
Whether the image has gold paint
Whether it is in a museum
questions.explanation: A careful response distinguishes veneration of an image as a witness from worship, which is due to God alone.

questions.prompt: “The resurrection is just a metaphor.” Which claim is central to apostolic preaching?
choices: A general feeling of renewal
Christ actually rose, grounding hope for the resurrection of the dead
The disciples invented a useful ritual
A ghost appeared
questions.explanation: Apostolic preaching centers on Christ actually rising and thereby grounding hope for the resurrection of the dead.

questions.prompt: “Orthodox Christians put Tradition above the Bible.” Which answer represents Orthodox teaching?
choices: The Bible is discarded
Scripture holds first place within the Church’s Holy Tradition
Every local custom has equal authority
Councils wrote the Bible before the apostles
questions.explanation: Orthodox teaching gives Scripture first place within Holy Tradition; Tradition is not a license to discard the Bible or equate every custom with apostolic teaching.

challenges.title: The case that Jesus is God
challenges.summary: Build a cumulative case from John, Paul, Hebrews, and the resurrection.
challenges.source: OCA · The Incarnation

lessons.heading: Start with the claim, not a slogan
lessons.body: Orthodoxy does not say Jesus is the Father. It says the one Jesus Christ is the eternal Son, personally distinct from the Father, sharing the divine nature and truly assuming a complete human nature. John 1:1 and 1:14 hold together distinction, divinity, and incarnation.

lessons.heading: Read John in its own sequence
lessons.body: John 1:1–3 puts the Word before created things, describes him as with God and as God, and says all things came to be through him. John 1:14 identifies that Word as the one who became flesh. John 20:28 records Thomas addressing the risen Jesus as “My Lord and my God.” John 17:3 records Jesus addressing the Father as the only true God. The Orthodox reading does not discard the last text; it distinguishes the Father from the Son without making the Son a creature.

lessons.heading: Read worship and divine identity together
lessons.body: Philippians 2:6–11 moves from Christ’s divine status through humiliation to his exaltation and universal confession as Lord, echoing Isaiah 45:23. Hebrews 1:8–12 addresses the Son with language of divine kingship and creation; its use of Psalm 102 warrants close reading in context. Colossians 1:16–17 and 2:9 present all creation in relation to him and the fullness of deity dwelling bodily in him. A cumulative argument is stronger than relying on a single ambiguous word.

lessons.heading: Handle the hard texts honestly
lessons.body: Jesus prays, learns, suffers, and says the Father is greater (John 14:28). These are genuine data, not verses to hide. The Incarnation means the Son acts and speaks in a real human life; passages of dependence must be read alongside texts of preexistence and divine identity. The argument requires a theological synthesis; it is not a mathematical proof forced by one verse.

furtherReading.label: Jehovah’s Witness position on the Trinity

questions.prompt: Which combination most directly underlies the Orthodox reading of John 1?
choices: Word created first, then promoted
Word with God, Word God, all things made through him, Word became flesh
Word only a metaphor for Scripture
Word and Father are the same Person
questions.explanation: John 1 joins the Word’s being with God, being God, creating all things, and becoming flesh.

questions.prompt: What does Thomas say to the risen Jesus in John 20:28?
choices: My teacher and prophet
My Lord and my God
You are the Father
You are an angel
questions.explanation: Thomas addresses the risen Jesus, “My Lord and my God,” in John 20:28.

questions.prompt: Why is Philippians 2:6–11 especially relevant?
choices: It denies Christ had a human life
It joins Christ’s prior status, humiliation, and universal confession as Lord
It identifies Mary as divine
It never mentions Jesus
questions.explanation: Philippians 2 joins Christ’s prior divine status, self-humbling, exaltation, and universal confession as Lord.

questions.prompt: What is the careful response to John 17:3, where Jesus calls the Father the only true God?
choices: Delete the verse
Admit the Father is distinct and ask how this fits John’s wider portrait of the Son
Say Jesus is the Father
Claim John 1 does not exist
questions.explanation: John 17:3 should not be deleted or twisted: the Father is distinct from the Son, and the verse must be read with John’s wider portrait of the Son.

questions.prompt: What does Hebrews 1 contribute to a cumulative case?
choices: It treats the Son as simply one of the angels
It contrasts the Son with angels and uses divine kingship and creator language for him
It denies the Old Testament
It proves the Father and Son are one Person
questions.explanation: Hebrews 1 contrasts the Son with angels and applies divine kingship and creator language to him.

questions.prompt: Why is one proof text alone often inadequate in a serious dialogue?
choices: Scripture is irrelevant
Translation, context, genre, and other passages must be considered
All readings are identical
Only councils may be cited
questions.explanation: Serious dialogue requires translation, context, genre, and the witness of other passages, not one isolated proof text.

questions.prompt: What does Chalcedonian Christology let us affirm about Jesus praying to the Father?
choices: He pretended to pray
His true human life and distinct sonship are real; prayer does not alone settle whether he shares the divine nature
The Father prayed to himself
His divinity disappeared
questions.explanation: Chalcedonian teaching lets Christ’s prayer be a real human act of the distinct Son; prayer by itself does not prove he is a creature.

questions.prompt: Which claim overstates the biblical argument?
choices: John 20:28 is relevant evidence
The New Testament portrays Jesus in relation to divine identity
One isolated English verse compels every reader to accept the entire later conciliar formula
John 1 links the Word to creation
questions.explanation: One isolated English verse does not by itself compel every reader to accept the entire later conciliar formula; the case is cumulative.

challenges.title: Proving the Trinity responsibly
challenges.summary: One God, distinct Father, Son, and Spirit: build the case without a bad analogy.
challenges.source: OCA · The Three Divine Persons

lessons.heading: Define the terms first
lessons.body: “One” answers what God is: the one divine nature. “Three” answers who: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The claim is not that one Person is three Persons, or that one nature is three natures. Analogies such as water changing states easily collapse the real distinction of Persons and are not proofs.

lessons.heading: Keep the Shema
lessons.body: Deuteronomy 6:4 confesses the Lord as one, and Jesus affirms the commandment in Mark 12:29. Trinitarian faith does not add gods to Israel’s God. Its question is how Jesus and the Spirit are spoken of within the worship and action of the one God. A Jewish reader can disagree with the Christian answer without being accused of denying the Shema.

lessons.heading: Follow the narrative
lessons.body: At Jesus’s baptism (Matthew 3:16–17), the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. In Matthew 28:19, baptism is into the singular name of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. John 14–16 speaks of the Son asking the Father to send the Paraclete. These texts support personal distinction; other texts establish the Son’s and Spirit’s divine life and action.

lessons.heading: Respect the limits of “proof”
lessons.body: The word “Trinity” is a later theological term. The developed vocabulary is not printed as a single New Testament sentence. The Christian case is an inference from multiple passages and the Church’s worship: one God, the Son’s divine identity, the Spirit’s personal divine action, and distinction among them. A serious defense explains each premise and its rival readings.

furtherReading.label: Chabad · Jewish understanding of divine unity

questions.prompt: What does “one nature, three Persons” distinguish?
choices: The number of gods from the number of churches
What God is from who God is
Old Testament from New Testament
Three phases in time
questions.explanation: “One” answers what God is, the one divine nature; “three” answers who God is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: Does the Orthodox argument reject Deuteronomy 6:4?
choices: Yes, it teaches three gods
No; it claims the one God is confessed as Father, Son, and Spirit
Yes, the Shema is obsolete
Only in the Gospel of John
questions.explanation: The Orthodox argument does not reject the Shema; it confesses the one God as Father, Son, and Spirit.

questions.prompt: What does the baptism scene in Matthew 3:16–17 most plainly show?
choices: Three gods
Father, Son, and Spirit are distinguishable in the narrative
Jesus is the Father
The Spirit is a dove by nature
questions.explanation: At the baptism, the Son is baptized, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks, so the three are distinguishable in the narrative.

questions.prompt: What is significant about Matthew 28:19?
choices: It names only Jesus
It names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in baptism
It denies monotheism
It lists three divine natures
questions.explanation: Matthew 28:19 gives baptism into the singular name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: Why is “one God playing three roles” inadequate?
choices: It makes three gods
It erases real personal distinction
It says the Son was created
It denies Jesus’s humanity
questions.explanation: One God playing three roles is inadequate because it erases the real distinction of the Persons.

questions.prompt: What is the honest response to “the word Trinity is absent from Scripture”?
choices: The word appears in John 1
The term is later; the question is whether it faithfully summarizes the scriptural witness
Vocabulary never matters
Scripture has no role
questions.explanation: “Trinity” is a later term; the issue is whether it faithfully summarizes the scriptural witness.

questions.prompt: Which reply to a Jewish objection about God’s oneness is most accurate?
choices: Judaism is secretly Trinitarian
The Shema matters to both traditions, but Jewish and Christian interpretations differ
The Hebrew Bible teaches three gods
Divine unity is irrelevant
questions.explanation: Both Jewish and Christian readers take the Shema seriously, while their interpretations of God’s unity and of Jesus differ.

questions.prompt: What is an important limit of the baptism scene by itself?
choices: It has no Father
It shows distinction, but additional texts and reasoning are needed to establish the full doctrine
It proves modalism
It says Jesus was not baptized
questions.explanation: The baptism scene shows distinction, but the full doctrine also needs texts and reasoning about unity, divinity, and worship.

challenges.title: Why the councils mattered
challenges.summary: Trace which question each council faced and what its answer did and did not say.
challenges.source: OCA · The Councils

lessons.heading: Nicaea I (325) and Constantinople I (381)
lessons.body: Nicaea I rejected the claim that the Son was made from nothing and confessed him of one essence with the Father. Constantinople I reaffirmed Nicene faith and defended the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Neither council claimed the Father and Son are one Person.

lessons.heading: Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451)
lessons.body: Ephesus insisted that Mary is Theotokos because the one she bore is the divine Son incarnate. Chalcedon confessed one and the same Christ in two complete natures, without confusion or division. “Two natures” is not “two Sons”; “one Person” does not erase his full humanity.

lessons.heading: Constantinople III (680–681) and Nicaea II (787)
lessons.body: The Sixth Council affirmed Christ’s divine and human wills, in accord with his two natures, without rivalry. Nicaea II defended icons and distinguished veneration from worship of God alone, tied to the reality of the Incarnation. Each decision addresses a different consequence of confessing the Word made flesh.

lessons.heading: Read councils as interpretive judgments
lessons.body: Councils did not create Jesus’s divinity by vote or add a new member to the Trinity. They used philosophical vocabulary to rule out interpretations they judged incompatible with apostolic faith. History still matters: ask which dispute a formula answered, what text was at stake, and where Christians outside Eastern Orthodoxy contest its reception.

furtherReading.label: OCA · The Incarnation and the councils

questions.prompt: Which issue did Nicaea I principally address?
choices: Whether the Son is a creature or fully divine
Whether icons can be photographed
Whether Paul wrote Romans
Whether monks may marry
questions.explanation: Nicaea I principally addressed whether the Son is a creature or fully divine.

questions.prompt: What did Constantinople I (381) clarify in Nicene faith?
choices: The Son has no human body
The Holy Spirit is divine and worshipped with Father and Son
Mary is divine
There are two gods
questions.explanation: Constantinople I clarified Nicene faith by confessing the Holy Spirit as divine, worshipped and glorified with the Father and the Son.

questions.prompt: Why did Ephesus insist on Theotokos?
choices: To say Mary is older than God
To preserve that the one born of her is the divine Son incarnate
To make two separate Sons
To replace the Gospel
questions.explanation: Ephesus used Theotokos to preserve that the one born of Mary is the divine Son incarnate, not a separate merely human son.

questions.prompt: Which formula is Chalcedonian?
choices: One Person, two complete natures
Two persons, one blended nature
One Person, one merely divine nature
Three persons in Christ
questions.explanation: The Chalcedonian formula is one Person in two complete natures.

questions.prompt: Why does the Sixth Council affirm two wills in Christ?
choices: Because there are two Sons
Because a complete human nature includes a human will, united without opposition to the divine will
Because God changes his mind
Because Jesus had no divine will
questions.explanation: The Sixth Council affirmed two natural wills because Christ’s complete human nature includes a human will, freely united without opposition to the divine will.

questions.prompt: What did Nicaea II (787) defend?
choices: Worship of wood
Veneration of icons, distinguished from worship due to God
That Christ was never visible
The rejection of all imagery
questions.explanation: Nicaea II defended veneration of icons while reserving worship to God alone.

questions.prompt: Which historical claim is too strong?
choices: Councils answered real disputes
Councils used conceptual language
A council vote first made Jesus divine
Council definitions aim to preserve apostolic faith
questions.explanation: A council did not make Jesus divine by voting; councils judged disputes and formulated safeguards for apostolic faith.

questions.prompt: What question helps interpret a conciliar formula accurately?
choices: Which emperor had the biggest army?
Which rival interpretation was the formula answering?
How short can a meme make it?
Can the history be ignored?
questions.explanation: A conciliar formula is read accurately by asking which rival interpretation it was answering.

challenges.title: Comparing religious objections fairly
challenges.summary: Engage Muslim, Jewish, and Jehovah’s Witness objections without misrepresenting their beliefs.
challenges.source: OCA · Trinity and Incarnation

lessons.heading: First understand the actual objection
lessons.body: The Qur’an 4:171 rejects saying “Trinity” and describes Jesus as a messenger; 5:72 rejects identifying the Messiah with God. Christian and Muslim readings thus differ at the identity of Jesus and the meaning of divine unity. Do not tell a Muslim that the Trinity is Father, Mary, and Jesus, or that divine begetting is physical. Those are not Orthodox claims.

lessons.heading: Jewish monotheism is a real disagreement
lessons.body: Traditional Jewish belief strongly affirms God’s unique, indivisible oneness and rejects Christian claims about Jesus. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) is central for both Jewish and Christian discussion. A Christian argument cannot simply assume that every Jewish use of “Lord” already means a Trinity; it must explain its reading of the New Testament and Israel’s Scriptures while admitting the other reading.

lessons.heading: Nontrinitarian Christian readings
lessons.body: Jehovah’s Witnesses reject the Trinity and distinguish Jesus from Almighty God, often appealing to John 17:3 and the Father’s primacy. Orthodoxy agrees that Father and Son are personally distinct but argues from John 1, John 20:28, Philippians 2, and Hebrews 1 that the Son is uncreated and truly divine. Discuss actual passages and translation choices rather than merely declaring the other side dishonest.

lessons.heading: What counts as a good case?
lessons.body: State the other position in terms its adherents recognize. Present a cumulative case, handle the strongest countertext, distinguish a historical fact from a theological interpretation, and say what your evidence cannot compel. “Proving” in apologetics means giving a reasoned defense, not pretending that disagreement disappears.

questions.prompt: What does Qur’an 4:171 explicitly reject?
choices: The existence of Jesus
The Trinity and divine sonship as understood in that text
The existence of Mary
All prophecy
questions.explanation: Qur’an 4:171 rejects saying “Trinity” and rejects divine sonship as presented there; it does not deny that Jesus or Mary existed.

questions.prompt: Which is a misrepresentation of Orthodox belief?
choices: The Son is distinct from the Father
The Trinity consists of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
Mary is a divine member of the Trinity
God is one
questions.explanation: Mary is not a divine member of the Trinity; that is a misrepresentation of Orthodox belief.

questions.prompt: What is a fair starting point for dialogue with a Jewish reader about the Shema?
choices: Say Jewish monotheism secretly teaches three gods
Affirm God’s oneness, then explain the distinct Christian claim about Jesus
Avoid the Hebrew Bible
Claim the Shema has no authority
questions.explanation: A fair start affirms God’s oneness in the Shema and then explains the distinct Christian claim about Jesus.

questions.prompt: What is a Jehovah’s Witness objection that should be engaged directly?
choices: Jesus never existed
John 17:3 calls the Father the only true God
Mary is the Holy Spirit
Icons were made in 325
questions.explanation: John 17:3, where Jesus calls the Father the only true God, is a direct objection that should be engaged rather than avoided.

questions.prompt: Which is the best treatment of a disputed translation in John 1:1?
choices: Insult the translator
Compare grammar, context, and how John 1:3 and 1:14 identify the Word
Skip the passage entirely
Say English words alone settle it
questions.explanation: A disputed translation is handled by comparing grammar and context, including how John 1:3 and 1:14 identify the Word.

questions.prompt: What can a council definition legitimately do in apologetics?
choices: Replace the scriptural evidence
Clarify how the Church resolved competing interpretations of Scripture
Force a non-Christian to accept its authority
Make the Son divine centuries later
questions.explanation: A council definition can clarify how the Church resolved competing interpretations of Scripture; it does not replace the scriptural evidence.

questions.prompt: Which answer to “God cannot have a son” accurately states Orthodox belief?
choices: God physically fathered a child
The Son’s eternal relation to the Father is not a physical act of procreation
Mary is the Father
There was a time the Son did not exist
questions.explanation: Orthodox sonship is an eternal relation, not physical procreation by God.

questions.prompt: How should you conclude a cumulative argument for Christ’s divinity?
choices: Every reader must agree after one verse
These texts and the Church’s reading form a coherent case, while rival interpretations should be answered honestly
History is irrelevant
A disagreement proves bad faith
questions.explanation: A cumulative argument should present a coherent case and answer rival interpretations honestly, not claim one verse ends all disagreement.

challenges.title: The Fathers on the Incarnation
challenges.summary: Read Athanasius, Maximus, Basil, and Gregory alongside Scripture.
challenges.source: Athanasius · On the Incarnation

questions.prompt: Why does Athanasius insist the Word truly took a mortal body?
choices: To cease being divine
To meet death in human life and overcome corruption
To appear human without becoming so
To avoid a real resurrection
questions.explanation: Athanasius insists the Word truly took a mortal body to meet death within human life and overcome corruption.

questions.prompt: What does Maximus’s defense of two wills protect?
choices: Two separate Christs
Christ’s complete human nature alongside his divinity
A conflict between two gods
A purely symbolic human life
questions.explanation: Maximus’s defense of two wills protects Christ’s complete human nature together with his divinity; it does not create two Christs.

questions.prompt: Which scene bears directly on Christ’s human willing?
choices: Gethsemane: “not as I will, but as thou wilt”
The tower of Babel
The golden calf
No biblical scene
questions.explanation: Gethsemane, “not as I will, but as thou wilt,” directly displays Christ’s human willing and obedience.

questions.prompt: Why did Gregory Nazianzen reject the claim that Jesus had no human mind?
choices: Minds cannot be healed
A humanity lacking a human mind would be incomplete and leave it unhealed
Jesus was only a human prophet
The body was unreal
questions.explanation: Gregory Nazianzen argued that a humanity lacking a human mind would be incomplete and that what is not assumed is not healed.

questions.prompt: How does Basil discuss the Spirit in relation to baptism?
choices: The Spirit is absent
The Spirit is named with Father and Son in the baptismal command
The Spirit is only a bird
The Spirit is the Father in disguise
questions.explanation: Basil argues from the baptismal naming of the Spirit with the Father and the Son.

questions.prompt: Which passage most directly says the Word became flesh?
choices: John 1:14
Psalm 1:1
Exodus 20:4
Job 1:1
questions.explanation: John 1:14 most directly says the Word became flesh.

questions.prompt: What is a fair way to present a Father’s view in a study note?
choices: Invent a quotation
Identify a specific work and distinguish paraphrase from quotation
Attribute all later theology to one verse
Remove the source
questions.explanation: A fair presentation identifies a specific work and distinguishes accurate paraphrase from exact quotation.

questions.prompt: Which claim best fits Maximus’s cosmic reading of Christ?
choices: Created life is irrelevant to salvation
Christ’s work concerns the healing and reconciliation of creation
The Word was created as part of the cosmos
All biblical numbers are secret codes
questions.explanation: Maximus reads Christ’s work as healing and reconciling creation, not treating created life as irrelevant.

challenges.title: Read the passage, test the claim
challenges.summary: Distinguish what the text says from later theological interpretation.

questions.prompt: What does Matthew 1:17 explicitly count?
choices: Three groups of fourteen generations
Fourteen apostles
Fourteen councils
A date for the Second Coming
questions.explanation: Matthew 1:17 explicitly counts three groups of fourteen generations.

questions.prompt: What is the status of connecting fourteen to the Hebrew numerical value of David?
choices: An explanation Matthew states outright
A plausible literary interpretation, not an explicit explanation in the Gospel

A claim about Luke’s genealogy

choices: Only the first line
The whole lament, including its movement toward praise
An unrelated genealogy
No Old Testament context

choices: They listen patiently
They assume suffering must reveal the sufferer’s guilt
They believe Job exists
They read poetry

choices: Genesis 12:3 and Galatians 3:8
Leviticus 11 and Revelation 13
Job 2 and Matthew 7
Exodus 3 and 1 John 5
questions.explanation: Genesis 12:3 promises blessing to the nations, and Galatians 3:8 connects that promise with the Gospel.

questions.prompt: How should the Good Samaritan shape a reader’s response?
choices: Identify only a theoretical neighbor
Practice mercy toward the person in need
Ignore the wounded man
Assume Samaritan and priest share the same role
questions.explanation: The Good Samaritan calls the reader to practice mercy toward the person in need, not merely define “neighbor.”

choices: Yes, always
No; he confronts mercyless religious practice

No, because the verse is in Revelation

questions.prompt: What is a responsible way to connect an Old Testament passage to Christ?
choices: Erase its historical setting
Read its setting and the New Testament use of it together
Treat every number as predictive
Claim the original text directly names modern events
questions.explanation: A responsible typological reading keeps the passage’s historical setting together with the New Testament’s use of it.

challenges.title: The full humanity of Christ
challenges.summary: Test the councils and the scriptural passages behind two natures and two wills.
challenges.source: OCA · The Sixth Ecumenical Council

questions.prompt: What did Chalcedon confess?
choices: One Person in two complete natures
Two unrelated sons
One blended nature with no distinction
A divine mind in an otherwise empty body
questions.explanation: Chalcedon confessed one Person in two complete natures.

questions.prompt: What did the Sixth Ecumenical Council affirm?
choices: No human will in Christ
Divine and human natural wills and activities in the one Christ
Two independent persons
Only a human will
questions.explanation: The Sixth Ecumenical Council affirmed divine and human natural wills and activities in the one Christ.

questions.prompt: Does affirming two wills mean Jesus was two people?
choices: Yes
No; the wills correspond to his two natures in one Person
Only before his baptism
Only in Revelation
questions.explanation: Two wills do not mean two people; the wills correspond to the two natures of the one Person.

questions.prompt: What makes the prayer in Gethsemane important?
choices: It shows pretend suffering
It shows genuine human obedience in the face of suffering
It denies the crucifixion
It proves the Father has a body
questions.explanation: Gethsemane shows genuine human obedience in the face of suffering, not pretend suffering.

questions.prompt: If Christ has no human mind, which patristic objection applies?
choices: Gregory’s argument that what is not assumed is not healed
Basil’s ban on reading
Maximus’s claim of three gods
Athanasius’s rejection of resurrection
questions.explanation: Gregory’s objection is the principle that what is not assumed is not healed.

questions.prompt: Which text says the Son shared flesh and blood?
choices: Hebrews 2:14
Genesis 1:1
Psalm 110:1
Deuteronomy 6:4
questions.explanation: Hebrews 2:14 says the Son shared flesh and blood.

questions.prompt: How does the Incarnation relate to icons in Orthodox theology?
choices: It forbids depicting Christ’s humanity
The Word truly became visible and can be depicted in his human life
It turns wood into a god
It makes every picture an icon
questions.explanation: Because the Word truly became visible, Christ can be depicted in his human life; matter is not turned into a god.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best avoids a false choice?
choices: Jesus was God, so his hunger was fake
Jesus was human, so he could not be divine
The one divine Son lived a genuine human life
Jesus became a different person at resurrection
questions.explanation: The best sentence avoids the false choice: the one divine Son lived a genuine human life.

challenges.title: One God, three Persons
challenges.summary: Learn a clear answer to the “three gods” objection.
challenges.source: OCA · The Holy Trinity

questions.prompt: A friend says, “Three Persons means three gods.” What do you clarify first?
choices: God is three beings
The three Persons share one divine nature
The Son is the Father
questions.explanation: The three Persons share one divine nature; “three Persons” does not mean three gods.

questions.prompt: At Jesus’s baptism, what does the Gospel show?
choices: The Son, Spirit, and Father are distinguishable
The Spirit is the Father in disguise
Three separate gods speak
questions.explanation: The baptism narrative distinguishes the Son, the Holy Spirit, and the Father.

questions.prompt: Does the word “Trinity” appear in the Bible?
choices: Yes, in Matthew 28:19
No; it is later language summarizing scriptural witness
No, so Christians invented God
questions.explanation: The word “Trinity” does not appear in Scripture; it is later language summarizing the scriptural witness.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest short reply?
choices: Three Persons = three natures
God is one; Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct Persons, not three gods
The Father alone is divine
questions.explanation: The strongest reply confesses one God and three distinct Persons, not three gods and not the Father alone.

challenges.title: Did God really become human?
challenges.summary: Trace the Word made flesh and answer the “only appeared human” claim.
challenges.source: Ignatius · To the Smyrnaeans

questions.prompt: Which line most directly affirms the Incarnation?
choices: The Word became flesh (John 1:14)
A wise man was later promoted to God
Jesus only seemed to have a body
questions.explanation: John 1:14, “The Word became flesh,” most directly affirms the Incarnation.

questions.prompt: Why does Ignatius insist Christ truly suffered?
choices: Because the passion was only a symbol
Because salvation concerns the real human life the Son assumed
Because Christ ceased to be divine
questions.explanation: Ignatius insists on Christ’s real suffering because salvation concerns the real human life the Son assumed.

questions.prompt: What does “Theotokos” protect?
choices: Mary originated God’s divine nature
The child born of Mary is the one divine Son incarnate
Mary is part of the Trinity
questions.explanation: Theotokos protects that the child born of Mary is the one divine Son incarnate.

questions.prompt: Jesus says, “Handle me and see.” Why does Luke include this?
choices: To deny resurrection
To show the risen Christ is bodily real, not a ghost
To say Christ lacked a human soul
questions.explanation: Luke’s “Handle me and see” shows the risen Christ is bodily real, not a ghost.

challenges.title: Answer without a straw man
challenges.summary: Practice careful replies to Muslim, Jewish, and nontrinitarian objections.
challenges.source: OCA · The Incarnation

questions.prompt: A Muslim objects that God cannot physically beget a son. What do you say?
choices: Orthodoxy means biological procreation
Eternal sonship is not physical reproduction
The Trinity includes Mary
questions.explanation: Eternal sonship is not physical reproduction; that answers the objection without caricaturing Orthodoxy.

questions.prompt: A Jewish friend cites the Shema: “The Lord is one.” What is a fair start?
choices: Say the Shema is false
Affirm God’s oneness and explain the Christian reading of Jesus
Claim Judaism teaches three gods
questions.explanation: A fair start affirms God’s oneness in the Shema and then explains the Christian reading of Jesus.

questions.prompt: Someone cites John 17:3 against Christ’s divinity. What next?
choices: Ignore it
Read it with John 1:1–14 and 20:28, distinguishing Father and Son
Say Jesus is the Father
questions.explanation: John 17:3 should be read with John 1:1–14 and John 20:28 while distinguishing the Father from the Son.

questions.prompt: What makes a good apologetic answer?
choices: A single verse taken out of context
Fairly state the objection, then give a contextual case
Assume disagreement proves bad faith
questions.explanation: A good answer fairly states the objection and gives a contextual case rather than leaning on one isolated verse.

challenges.title: The Islamic Dilemma
challenges.summary: The Quran affirms the Bible — and disagrees with it. Learn the two horns and the one question that opens the conversation.
challenges.source: The Quran · the early manuscripts · St. John of Damascus

lessons.heading: The setup: the Quran points to the Bible
lessons.body: The Quran calls the Torah and the Gospel God's revealed books. It tells Jews to judge by the Torah and Christians by the Gospel (Q 5:43-47), tells Muhammad, if he is in doubt, to ask those who read the Scripture before him (Q 10:94), and insists no one can change the words of God (Q 6:115; 18:27). On its own terms, then, the Bible is a standing witness — not a broken one.

lessons.heading: Horn one: if the Bible stands, the Quran falls
lessons.body: We can check what the Bible said in Muhammad's day, because our copies are older than Islam: the Dead Sea Scrolls predate Christ, and Codex Sinaiticus (about AD 350) gives us the whole New Testament more than two centuries before Muhammad (AD 570-632). That Bible proclaims the crucifixion and Jesus as the Son of God; the Quran denies both (Q 4:157; 5:72). If the Bible the Quran praised is this Bible, then on the contested points the Quran fails by the witness it chose.

lessons.heading: Horn two: 'it was corrupted' — when?
lessons.body: The usual answer is tahrif: the text was corrupted. Press one question: when? If before Muhammad, the Quran praised a corrupted book and called God's words unchangeable. If after Muhammad, the manuscripts answer: copies older than his lifetime already read as ours do. St. John of Damascus, the first Christian writer to answer Islam (he died about AD 749), already treated it as a splinter off Christianity — this conversation is nearly as old as Islam itself. Keep the aim narrow: we are testing a book's own claims, not attacking the person in front of us.

questions.prompt: What does the Quran tell Christians to judge by?
choices: Their own church traditions
The Gospel in their hands (Q 5:47)
Only the Quran
questions.explanation: Q 5:47: 'Let the People of the Gospel judge by what God has revealed therein.' The Quran sends Christians back to their Gospel as a living standard.

questions.prompt: A friend says the Bible was corrupted (tahrif). What is the cleanest first question?
choices: 'Which church do you attend?'
'Why do you pray five times a day?'
'Corrupted when — before or after Muhammad?'
questions.explanation: Timing is the dilemma. 'Before Muhammad' clashes with the Quran praising the earlier Scripture and calling God's words unchangeable (Q 6:115). 'After Muhammad' collides with the manuscript record.

questions.prompt: Why do Codex Sinaiticus and the Dead Sea Scrolls matter in this argument?
choices: They are the first two churches
They prove the biblical text existed centuries before Islam, matching what we read now
They were written by Muhammad's followers
questions.explanation: Sinaiticus (about AD 350) and the Scrolls (before Christ) predate Islam by centuries, so the Bible of Muhammad's day is checkable — and it proclaims the crucifixion and the Son.

challenges.title: Genesis: beginnings and promise
challenges.summary: Creation, the human image, and Abraham’s promise.
challenges.source: Genesis 1–3; 12:1–3

lessons.heading: The book
lessons.body: Orthodox reading receives Genesis as the beginning of creation and God’s covenant story. The same God who creates also seeks humanity after the fall.

lessons.heading: The image
lessons.body: St Athanasius reads humanity made in God’s image in light of the Word who comes to renew that image. See Genesis 1:26–27 and John 1:14.

lessons.heading: The promise
lessons.body: God calls Abraham and promises blessing to the families of the earth. Paul connects that promise with the Gospel in Galatians 3:8.

questions.prompt: What does Genesis say God saw after creating?
choices: That it was good
That it was finished by Adam
That it was hidden
questions.explanation: Genesis repeatedly says God saw that creation was good.

questions.prompt: Where does Genesis say humanity is made in God’s image?
choices: Genesis 1:26–27
Genesis 12:3
Genesis 50:20
questions.explanation: Genesis 1:26–27 says humanity is made in God’s image.

questions.prompt: Who receives the promise of blessing for all families of the earth?
choices: Abraham
Pharaoh
Goliath
questions.explanation: Abraham receives the promise that all families of the earth will be blessed in him.

challenges.title: The Gospels: Christ’s life and Pascha
challenges.summary: Four witnesses, incarnation, and resurrection.
challenges.source: John 1; Luke 24

lessons.heading: Four Gospels
lessons.body: Orthodox reading receives Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John as four witnesses to one Lord. Each tells the good news of Jesus Christ.

lessons.heading: The Word made flesh
lessons.body: St Athanasius stresses that the eternal Word truly took our humanity. John 1:14 speaks of the incarnation, not an appearance or disguise.

lessons.heading: Pascha
lessons.body: The risen Christ meets Mary Magdalene and the disciples. Luke 24 and John 20 narrate encounters, not merely a remembered idea.

questions.prompt: Which list names all four canonical Gospels?
choices: Matthew, Mark, Luke, John
Matthew, Acts, Romans, John
Genesis, Mark, Luke, Acts
questions.explanation: The four canonical Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

questions.prompt: What does John 1:14 say?
choices: The Word was made flesh
The Word stopped existing
The Word was only an angel
questions.explanation: John 1:14 says the Word was made flesh.

questions.prompt: Where does Luke tell of two disciples meeting the risen Jesus?
choices: On the road to Emmaus
At Mount Sinai
At the Red Sea
questions.explanation: Luke tells of two disciples meeting the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus.

challenges.title: The Psalms: prayer and prophecy
challenges.summary: Pray the Psalter and navigate its two numbering systems.
challenges.source: Psalms 22–23

lessons.heading: A book of prayer
lessons.body: Orthodox worship prays the Psalms as the Church’s own speech before God: lament, praise, repentance, and hope.

lessons.heading: Two numberings
lessons.body: The KJV follows Hebrew numbering; the Septuagint Psalter used in Orthodox worship often differs. KJV Psalm 23 is LXX Psalm 22.

lessons.heading: Read with Christ
lessons.body: Jesus quotes Psalm 22 at the cross. Read the whole lament, including its turn toward praise, before drawing conclusions from one line.

questions.prompt: What is the Septuagint number of KJV Psalm 23?
questions.explanation: In Septuagint numbering, KJV Psalm 23 is Psalm 22.

questions.prompt: Which Psalm begins “The Lord is my shepherd” in KJV numbering?
choices: Psalm 23
Psalm 2
Psalm 119
questions.explanation: KJV Psalm 23 begins, “The Lord is my shepherd.”

questions.prompt: Which Psalm opens with a cry Jesus quotes on the cross?
choices: Psalm 22
Psalm 150
Psalm 1
questions.explanation: Psalm 22 opens with the cry Jesus quotes on the cross.

challenges.title: Nicaea I · 325
challenges.summary: The Son is truly God, not a creature.
challenges.source: OCA · Fourth Century, First Ecumenical Council

lessons.heading: The question
lessons.body: Orthodox confession follows the apostolic witness that the Son is eternal and fully divine. Nicaea rejected the claim that the Son was created.

lessons.heading: The witness
lessons.body: St Athanasius points to John 1:1–3: the Word was God and all things were made through him. The creator does not belong among created things.

lessons.heading: The confession
lessons.body: The council confessed the Son as of one essence with the Father. Its language guards the scriptural witness rather than inventing a new Son.

questions.prompt: What claim did Nicaea I reject?
choices: The Son was created
Christ became flesh
God created the world
questions.explanation: Nicaea I rejected the claim that the Son was created.

questions.prompt: Which passage calls the Word God and says all things were made through him?
choices: John 1:1–3
Jonah 1:1–3
Ruth 1:1–3
questions.explanation: John 1:1–3 calls the Word God and says all things were made through him.

questions.prompt: What did Nicaea confess about the Son and Father?
choices: One divine essence
Two separate gods
One person wearing masks
questions.explanation: Nicaea confessed the Son and the Father to be of one divine essence.

challenges.title: Constantinople I · 381
challenges.summary: The Holy Spirit is Lord and giver of life.
challenges.source: OCA · Fourth Century, Second Ecumenical Council

lessons.heading: The confession
lessons.body: Orthodox worship glorifies the Spirit together with the Father and the Son. Constantinople I clarified the Nicene confession of the Holy Spirit.

lessons.heading: Scripture
lessons.body: Matthew 28:19 names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in baptism. Acts 5:3–4 speaks gravely of lying to the Spirit and to God.

lessons.heading: The Father
lessons.body: St Basil’s On the Holy Spirit argues from baptism and worship that the Spirit is not a creature or an afterthought.

questions.prompt: Who is named in the baptismal command?
choices: Father, Son, Holy Spirit
Father, Moses, Elijah
Peter, Paul, John
questions.explanation: The baptismal command names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

questions.prompt: What does the Creed call the Spirit?
choices: Lord and giver of life
A created angel
A second savior
questions.explanation: The Creed calls the Holy Spirit Lord and giver of life.

questions.prompt: Which Father wrote On the Holy Spirit?
choices: Basil the Great
Arius
Nestorius
questions.explanation: Basil the Great wrote On the Holy Spirit.

challenges.title: Ephesus · 431
challenges.summary: Mary is Theotokos because her Son is the divine Word incarnate.
challenges.source: OCA · Fifth Century, Third Ecumenical Council

lessons.heading: One Christ
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching calls Mary Theotokos because the one she bore is the divine Son made flesh. The title identifies her Son; it does not make Mary the source of divinity.

lessons.heading: The Gospel
lessons.body: John 1:14 says the Word became flesh; Luke 1:43 records Elizabeth calling Mary the mother of her Lord.

lessons.heading: The Father
lessons.body: St Cyril of Alexandria defended the unity of the incarnate Christ against splitting him into two personal subjects.

questions.prompt: What does Theotokos protect?
choices: The identity of Mary’s Son as the divine Word incarnate
Mary as a fourth divine person
A claim that God began to exist
questions.explanation: Theotokos protects the identity of Mary’s Son as the divine Word incarnate.

questions.prompt: Which Gospel verse says the Word became flesh?
choices: John 1:14
John 11:35
Mark 1:1
questions.explanation: John 1:14 says the Word became flesh.

questions.prompt: Which Father defended Christ’s unity at Ephesus?
choices: Cyril of Alexandria
Arius
Nestorius
questions.explanation: Cyril of Alexandria defended Christ’s unity at Ephesus.

challenges.title: Chalcedon · 451
challenges.summary: One Christ in two complete natures.
challenges.source: OCA · Fifth Century, Fourth Ecumenical Council

lessons.heading: One Lord
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching confesses one Jesus Christ, fully divine and fully human, without dividing him into two persons or confusing his natures.

lessons.heading: The Gospel
lessons.body: John 1:14 speaks of the Word becoming flesh; Philippians 2:6–8 speaks of the Son taking the form of a servant.

lessons.heading: The Fathers
lessons.body: St Cyril’s emphasis on the one incarnate Son and the Fathers’ insistence on real humanity both shape careful reading of Chalcedon.

questions.prompt: How many persons does Chalcedon confess in Christ?
choices: One
Two
Three
questions.explanation: Chalcedon confesses one Person in Christ.

questions.prompt: Which natures are complete in Christ?
choices: Divine and human
Angelic and human
Only divine
questions.explanation: The complete natures in Christ are divine and human.

questions.prompt: Which passage speaks of the form of a servant?
choices: Philippians 2:7
Genesis 1:1
Psalm 1:1
questions.explanation: Philippians 2:7 speaks of Christ taking the form of a servant.

challenges.title: Constantinople II · 553
challenges.summary: The one born of Mary is the eternal Son.
challenges.source: OCA · Sixth Century, Fifth Ecumenical Council

lessons.heading: The same Christ
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching safeguards the unity of Christ: the one who lived and suffered in the flesh is the eternal Son, not a separate human person joined to him.

lessons.heading: Scripture
lessons.body: John 1:14 and 1 Corinthians 2:8 place the divine Lord and his real historical suffering in one Gospel confession.

lessons.heading: The Fathers
lessons.body: The council reaffirmed St Cyril of Alexandria’s insistence that one incarnate Word is the subject of Christ’s acts.

questions.prompt: Whose unity did Constantinople II defend?
choices: The one incarnate Christ
Two unrelated saviors
A merely human teacher
questions.explanation: Constantinople II defended the unity of the one incarnate Christ.

questions.prompt: Which verse says the Word was made flesh?
choices: John 1:14
Psalm 150:1
Acts 2:2
questions.explanation: John 1:14 says the Word was made flesh.

questions.prompt: Which Father’s Christological teaching was reaffirmed?
choices: Cyril of Alexandria
Arius
Nestorius
questions.explanation: The council reaffirmed Cyril of Alexandria’s Christological teaching.

challenges.title: Constantinople III · 680–681
challenges.summary: Christ has divine and human natural wills.
challenges.source: OCA · Seventh Century, Maximus the Confessor

lessons.heading: Complete humanity
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching confesses that Christ’s full humanity includes a human will. His human willing freely follows the divine will, never opposing it in sin.

lessons.heading: The prayer
lessons.body: In Matthew 26:39, Christ prays in Gethsemane, “not as I will, but as thou wilt.” Read his human obedience without splitting him into two persons.

lessons.heading: The Father
lessons.body: St Maximus the Confessor defended the two natural wills and activities of the one Christ before the Sixth Council.

questions.prompt: How many natural wills did the Sixth Council confess in Christ?
choices: Two, divine and human
Only one human will
Three opposing wills
questions.explanation: The Sixth Council confessed two natural wills in Christ, divine and human.

questions.prompt: Where does Christ pray “not as I will, but as thou wilt”?
choices: Matthew 26:39
Genesis 1:1
Psalm 23:1
questions.explanation: Matthew 26:39 records Christ praying, “not as I will, but as thou wilt.”

questions.prompt: Which Father defended Christ’s complete human willing?
choices: Maximus the Confessor
Arius
Nestorius
questions.explanation: Maximus the Confessor defended Christ’s complete human willing.

challenges.title: Nicaea II · 787
challenges.summary: Icons point to the incarnate Christ; worship belongs to God.
challenges.source: OCA · Seventh Ecumenical Council

lessons.heading: The image
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching allows Christ to be depicted because the Word truly became visible in the flesh. An icon witnesses to the one depicted.

lessons.heading: The distinction
lessons.body: Nicaea II distinguishes the honor given to an icon from worship, which belongs to God alone. John 1:14 anchors the argument in the incarnation.

lessons.heading: The Father
lessons.body: St John of Damascus defended holy images by pointing to the God who had become visible in human life.

questions.prompt: What makes an icon of Christ possible in Orthodox teaching?
choices: The Word truly became flesh
The Father is a wooden object
All materials are divine
questions.explanation: An icon of Christ is possible because the Word truly became flesh and visible.

questions.prompt: Who receives worship in Orthodox teaching?
choices: God alone
Every painted board
The artist
questions.explanation: Worship belongs to God alone; icons receive veneration, not worship.

questions.prompt: Which Father argued from the incarnation for icons?
choices: John of Damascus
Arius
Nestorius
questions.explanation: John of Damascus argued from the Incarnation for holy icons.

challenges.title: The words themselves: essence, person, nature
challenges.summary: Learn what ousia, hypostasis, and physis mean before using them to explain God and Christ.
challenges.source: Cappadocian Fathers · OCA · The Three Divine Persons

lessons.heading: Start with the question being asked
lessons.body: The Fathers use different words because they are answering different questions. Ousia asks what something is: God is one divine essence. Hypostasis asks who someone is: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Physis means nature, the kind of being and the capacities that belong to it. Keep the questions separate and the terms stay clear.

lessons.heading: A hypostasis is a real who
lessons.body: A hypostasis is a concrete, distinct subject: someone who truly exists and acts. In God there are three Hypostases. They are not parts of God, not competing individuals, and not three separate centers of divinity. The Cappadocians, including Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nyssa, and Gregory the Theologian, guarded both the real distinction of the Persons and the unity of God.

lessons.heading: Physis names a nature
lessons.body: Physis and ousia can overlap, so context matters. Speaking of God, one physis means one divine nature. Speaking of Christ, he has two physeis: complete divinity and complete humanity. A nature is not automatically a separate person. Nature answers what kind of life and powers someone has; hypostasis identifies who is acting.

questions.prompt: When you say God has one ousia, what are you talking about?
choices: One Person wearing three temporary masks
The one divine essence shared by Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
Three separate divine beings
questions.explanation: Ousia names what God is. Orthodoxy confesses one undivided divine essence, not three gods and not one Person acting under three temporary masks.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses hypostasis correctly?
choices: God changes from one hypostasis into another
Jesus has two hypostases because he has two natures
The Father is one Hypostasis, and the Son is another distinct Hypostasis
questions.explanation: Father and Son are distinct Hypostases. God does not change from one Person into another, and Christ is not two persons because he has two natures.

questions.prompt: What mistake should you avoid with the word nature?
choices: Saying Christ's humanity is unreal
Treating every nature as automatically a separate person
Using nature to answer what kind of being someone is
questions.explanation: A nature answers the question what, but it does not by itself settle who is acting. That distinction lets the Church confess one Christ with real divine and human natures.

challenges.title: One God in three Hypostases
challenges.summary: Confess homoousios, the Father as source, and perichoresis without falling into modalism, subordinationism, or tritheism.
challenges.source: Athanasius and John of Damascus · OCA · The Holy Trinity

lessons.heading: Homoousios: the Son is truly God
lessons.body: Nicaea calls the Son homoousios with the Father: of the same essence. Athanasius defended this against Arius because a creature, however exalted, could not unite humanity to God or grant divine life. The Son is not a lesser second God; he is truly God from truly God.

lessons.heading: The Father is the source
lessons.body: Orthodoxy speaks of the Father as the one source within the Trinity. The Son is eternally begotten of the Father, and the Holy Spirit eternally proceeds from the Father. Begotten and proceeding describe eternal relations, not events in time. Being from the Father does not make the Son or the Spirit lower in essence, glory, or divinity.

lessons.heading: Perichoresis: communion without confusion
lessons.body: John of Damascus uses perichoresis for the mutual indwelling of the divine Persons. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct, yet they are never separate, divided, or acting as three independent gods. Their unity is not a blur: the Persons remain distinct while sharing one undivided divine life.

questions.prompt: What does homoousios protect?
choices: The Son is the highest creature
The Son is of the same essence as the Father
The Father becomes the Son at the baptism of Jesus
questions.explanation: Homoousios means of the same essence. It rejects Arianism: the Son is not created or lesser in divinity, but truly God together with the Father.

questions.prompt: Which wording keeps the Father as source without subordinationism?
choices: The Son began later and is less divine
The Father is one mode that the Son later replaces
The Son is eternally from the Father and fully God
questions.explanation: The Son is eternally begotten of the Father, so there was never a time when the Son was not. Eternal origin does not mean inferior essence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids both modalism and tritheism?
choices: The three are three independent beings who cooperate
Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are distinct Persons who are never separate gods
Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one Person appearing in three roles
questions.explanation: The first choice divides God into three beings, and the third turns the Persons into roles or masks. Orthodox teaching confesses three distinct Hypostases, one essence, and one undivided divine life.

challenges.title: The hypostatic union: one Christ, two natures
challenges.summary: Use Chalcedon's guardrails to confess one hypostasis of God the Word in complete divinity and complete humanity.
challenges.source: Cyril of Alexandria and Chalcedon · OCA · Fifth Century

lessons.heading: One who, two whats
lessons.body: In the Incarnation, the one hypostasis of God the Word becomes man without ceasing to be God. He does not join himself to a separate human person. From the Theotokos he assumes complete human nature, including a real body and a rational human soul, and makes that humanity his own.

lessons.heading: Chalcedon's four guardrails
lessons.body: Chalcedon confesses Christ in two natures asynchytos, without confusion; atreptos, without change; adiairetos, without division; and achoristos, without separation. These are fences around the mystery. The natures are not blended into a hybrid, divinity is not altered, Christ is not split into two sons, and the union is not temporary or loose.

lessons.heading: Complete humanity, complete divinity
lessons.body: Cyril of Alexandria guards the unity of Christ, while Maximus the Confessor and the later councils guard his complete humanity. Christ has a real rational human mind and will; his humanity is not swallowed by divinity. He is not a divine appearance, not a body animated directly by divinity instead of a human soul, and not a mixture that leaves him neither fully God nor fully man.

questions.prompt: Who is the subject born of Mary?
choices: A separate human person later adopted by God
God the Word, now truly incarnate
A divine appearance without real humanity
questions.explanation: The one born of Mary is personally God the Son made man. A separate adopted human person would divide Christ, while a mere appearance would be Docetism.

questions.prompt: What does asynchytos, without confusion, rule out?
choices: Splitting Christ into two persons
Confusing the natures into a third hybrid nature
Calling Christ fully human
questions.explanation: Asynchytos rejects the Eutychian confusion of the natures. Christ remains fully God and fully man; the union does not blend divinity and humanity into something else.

questions.prompt: Which claim avoids both Apollinarianism and Eutychianism?
choices: His divinity replaces his human mind, and his humanity is absorbed
He only seems to eat, suffer, and die
He has a real rational human mind, and his humanity remains truly human
questions.explanation: Apollinarianism removes Christ's rational human mind, Eutychianism absorbs or confuses his humanity, and Docetism makes his embodied life only an appearance. The third sentence keeps his humanity complete and real.

challenges.title: Saying it right out loud
challenges.summary: Practice sentences with Theotokos, communicatio idiomatum, and one subject for all of Christ's actions.
challenges.source: Cyril of Alexandria · OCA · The Incarnation

lessons.heading: Theotokos protects who was born
lessons.body: The Church calls Mary Theotokos, Birth-giver of God, because the child she bore is personally God the Word made flesh. The title does not mean Mary created the divine nature or existed before God. It safeguards the unity of Christ: the same Son who is eternally begotten of the Father is born of Mary in the flesh.

lessons.heading: Speak of one subject, carefully
lessons.body: Communicatio idiomatum means that, because Christ is one subject, we may predicate human experiences of God the Word according to the flesh and divine works of the man Jesus according to his divinity. It does not transfer properties between the natures. When we say God suffered in the flesh, we mean the divine Person truly suffered in his human nature; the divine nature did not become passible by nature.

lessons.heading: Keep the same Jesus in every sentence
lessons.body: The same Lord hungers and feeds the multitude, prays and forgives sins, dies and rises. Do not assign the human actions to a separate man and the divine actions to a separate God beside him. Maximus the Confessor and John of Damascus keep both truths together: one incarnate Son acting in complete divinity and complete humanity.

questions.prompt: Why does the Church call Mary Theotokos?
choices: Because Mary is the source of Christ's divinity
Because Mary became a fourth divine Person
Because the child born of her is personally God the Son made man
questions.explanation: Theotokos is first a claim about Christ. Mary did not create the divine nature; she truly gave birth, in the flesh, to the eternal Son who made that humanity his own.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses communicatio idiomatum carefully?
choices: The divine nature changed into passible flesh
God the Word suffered in the flesh, while the divine nature did not become passible by nature
Only a separate human person suffered, not the Son
questions.explanation: Because the sufferer is personally God the Word, Scripture can say the Lord of glory was crucified. The suffering is real in the flesh; the divine nature is not changed into a passible nature.

questions.prompt: Pick the orthodox sentence.
choices: Jesus is a human person inspired by a separate divine Person
Christ is a mixture, neither fully God nor fully man
The same Jesus Christ is fully God and fully man, one Person acting in both natures
questions.explanation: The first sentence divides Christ into two persons, and the second confuses the natures into a mixture. The third keeps one subject and confesses complete divinity and complete humanity.

challenges.title: Asking the saints to pray for us
challenges.summary: A biblical defense of asking the departed saints for intercession without turning prayer into worship or necromancy.
challenges.source: Revelation 5:8; 8:3-4 · Hebrews 12:1 · 1 Timothy 2:1-5 · the early Church

lessons.heading: The departed saints are alive in Christ
lessons.body: The defense begins with life, not with death. Christ says God is not the God of the dead, but of the living (Luke 20:37-38). Hebrews places us before a great cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1), and Revelation shows the martyrs conscious before God, crying out for justice (Revelation 6:9-10). If the saints live in Christ, asking them to pray is not trying to reach people who vanished; it is asking living members of Christ's body to do what living Christians are told to do.

lessons.heading: Scripture commands intercession and pictures it in heaven
lessons.body: Paul commands that intercessions be made for all people (1 Timothy 2:1-3), and James says the prayer of a righteous person has great power (James 5:16). Revelation gives the same pattern a heavenly picture: the elders hold golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints (Revelation 5:8), and an angel offers incense with the prayers of all the saints before the throne (Revelation 8:3-4). Asking a saint to pray is not a new kind of religion; it is intercession received inside the communion of Christ.

lessons.heading: Not worship, and not necromancy
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching keeps the line clean: worship, latreia, belongs to God alone. Honor toward the saints, often called dulia, is the honor given to God's friends and members of Christ. Necromancy seeks hidden knowledge or control from the dead; the Church asks the saints for prayer to God. Christ remains the one mediator between God and man by nature (1 Timothy 2:5), while His members share in intercession by grace, just as they do on earth.

questions.prompt: In Revelation 5:8, the incense in the golden bowls is identified as what?
choices: The praises of angels only
The prayers of the saints
The smoke of the temple altar
The merits of the apostles
questions.explanation: Revelation 5:8 calls the incense the prayers of the saints. That image gives a biblical frame for heavenly intercession.

questions.prompt: What is the clean distinction when Orthodox Christians ask a saint to pray?
choices: Saints receive latreia because they are lesser gods
The saint replaces Christ as mediator by nature
We ask a living member of Christ to intercede, while worship belongs to God alone
The dead are contacted for secret information
questions.explanation: Asking for intercession is not worship and not necromancy. Christ alone is mediator by nature; His members intercede by grace.

questions.prompt: Why does 1 Timothy 2:5 not cancel 1 Timothy 2:1?
choices: Because Paul commands intercessions in the same passage where he names Christ the one mediator
Because mediator means only an earthly priest
Because saints are mediators by nature too
Because prayer to God is optional after baptism
questions.explanation: Paul's own order matters: intercessions are commanded first, then Christ is confessed as the one mediator. Shared prayer does not compete with His unique mediation.

challenges.title: Calling Mary Theotokos
challenges.summary: Why God-bearer is first a confession about Jesus: the child born of Mary is truly God the Word made flesh.
challenges.source: Luke 1:43 · John 1:1-14 · Galatians 4:4 · St. Cyril of Alexandria and Ephesus, 431

lessons.heading: Elizabeth already calls her the mother of my Lord
lessons.body: When Mary visits Elizabeth, Elizabeth cries out, why is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? (Luke 1:43). In that setting, Lord is not a polite title for a merely human baby. The question is not first about Mary. It is about who the child is. If the child in her womb is the Lord, then Mary is rightly named by relation to Him.

lessons.heading: The Word became flesh; the Son was born of a woman
lessons.body: John confesses that the Word was God and that the Word became flesh (John 1:1, 14). Paul says God sent forth his Son, born of a woman (Galatians 4:4). The Church does not say Mary created the divine nature. She bore, according to the flesh, the one Person who is God the Son. The word Theotokos means God-bearer; it guards the unity of Jesus Christ against splitting Him into God over here and a separate man over there.

lessons.heading: Ephesus protected Christ, not a rivalry with Him
lessons.body: At Ephesus in 431, St. Cyril of Alexandria defended Theotokos because denying it threatened the confession that Emmanuel is truly God. The title does not make Mary the source of the Trinity. It says that the same Son who is eternally begotten of the Father was truly born of Mary in time. Keep the phrase according to the flesh close by: Mary is mother of God incarnate, not mother of divinity as an abstract nature.

questions.prompt: What does Elizabeth call Mary in Luke 1:43?
choices: The mother of my Lord
The queen above the Trinity
The mother of a prophet only
The source of the divine nature
questions.explanation: Luke 1:43 gives the biblical seed of the title: mother of my Lord. The title follows from the identity of the child.

questions.prompt: What danger does the title Theotokos guard against?
choices: Saying Jesus had a real mother
Splitting Christ into a separate God and a separate man loosely joined together
Calling Mary blessed among women
Confessing that Christ was born in Bethlehem
questions.explanation: Theotokos protects the one Person of Christ. It refuses a Jesus who is partly attached to God from outside.

questions.prompt: What does Theotokos not mean?
choices: Mary bore God the Word according to the flesh
Jesus is truly God and truly man
Mary is the origin or creator of the divine nature
Elizabeth spoke by the Holy Spirit
questions.explanation: Mary did not create divinity. She bore the divine Son in His incarnation, so the title confesses Christ without exaggerating Mary into a source of Godhead.
