challenges.title: The true Body and Blood
challenges.summary: Why Orthodox Christians receive the Eucharist as real communion in Christ's Body and Blood, not as a bare reminder.
challenges.source: Matthew 26:26-28 · John 6:53-56 · 1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:23-29 · St. Ignatius of Antioch

lessons.heading: Take the words of institution at full weight
lessons.body: At the Mystical Supper Christ does not say, this only pictures my body. He says, This is my body, and, This is my blood of the new covenant (Matthew 26:26-28). Paul hands on the same words as a received tradition and warns the Corinthians to examine themselves and discern the body (1 Corinthians 11:23-29). A defense can be simple: the Church believes the Eucharist is what Christ calls it, received by faith in the mystery He gives.

lessons.heading: John 6 and the language of participation
lessons.body: In John 6 Christ says His flesh is true food and His blood is true drink, and that the one who eats and drinks abides in Him. Paul uses the word koinonia for the cup and the bread: a participation or communion in the blood and body of Christ (1 Corinthians 10:16). That is stronger than a mental reminder. Communion joins the faithful to Christ and to one another in His body.

lessons.heading: Real, sacramental, and approached with fear and faith
lessons.body: Orthodox teaching does not reduce the mystery to a laboratory object, and it does not turn the Eucharist into crude cannibalism. The gifts are truly the Body and Blood of Christ by the action of the Holy Spirit, received sacramentally under the forms of bread and wine. St. Ignatius of Antioch already called the Eucharist the medicine of immortality. Because the gift is real, Paul joins communion to repentance, reconciliation, and discernment.

questions.prompt: In 1 Corinthians 10:16, Paul calls the cup and bread a participation in what?
choices: A church picnic and a memory aid
The blood and body of Christ
The opinions of the Corinthians
A symbol with no gift given
questions.explanation: Paul's word is koinonia: participation or communion. The cup is participation in the blood of Christ; the bread is participation in the body of Christ.

questions.prompt: Which words of Christ stand behind the Orthodox defense?
choices: This represents my body from a distance
This is my body; this is my blood
This is only a teaching illustration
Do this until symbols are no longer useful
questions.explanation: The institution words are the anchor: This is my body, and, This is my blood. Orthodoxy receives them as gift and mystery, not as a bare sign.

questions.prompt: What does a reverent defense avoid claiming?
choices: That communion is a real participation in Christ
That the Eucharist is a crude physical object lesson rather than a sacramental mystery
That believers should examine themselves before communion
That John 6 speaks of eating and drinking
questions.explanation: The defense is real but not crude. Orthodoxy confesses the true Body and Blood while receiving the mystery sacramentally, with repentance and faith.

challenges.title: Essence and energies: truly knowing God
challenges.summary: How St. Gregory Palamas defended real participation in God's life while guarding that the divine essence remains beyond creatures.
challenges.source: Exodus 33 · Matthew 17 · Psalm 36:9 · 2 Peter 1:4 · St. Gregory Palamas

lessons.heading: The Bible holds two truths together
lessons.body: Moses asks to see God's glory and hears that no one can see God's face and live (Exodus 33:20). Paul says God dwells in unapproachable light (1 Timothy 6:16). Yet the same Bible says God reveals Himself, saves, fills, and gives life. A Christian answer has to protect both: God is not a creature we can comprehend, and God is not absent from the creatures He saves.

lessons.heading: Tabor shows uncreated light, and Peter speaks of participation
lessons.body: At the Transfiguration the disciples see Christ shining with divine glory (Matthew 17:1-8). The Psalm says, in thy light shall we see light (Psalm 36:9). Peter says believers become partakers of the divine nature (2 Peter 1:4). Orthodoxy reads these together: grace is not a created thing placed between us and God. It is God's own life and glory given to creatures, often named His energies.

lessons.heading: Palamas: essence beyond us, energies truly God with us
lessons.body: St. Gregory Palamas defended the hesychast monks by teaching a real distinction: God's essence is what God is in Himself and remains imparticipable to creatures; God's energies are His uncreated activities and life, truly God going forth to create, illumine, and deify. This is not two gods and not a created buffer. We participate in God by grace through His energies, while we never become God by essence.

questions.prompt: In the essence-energies distinction, what remains imparticipable to creatures?
choices: God's essence
God's energies
God's glory at Tabor
The life given in grace
questions.explanation: Palamas guards divine transcendence: creatures never comprehend or participate in God's essence as what God is in Himself.

questions.prompt: What do believers participate in by grace?
choices: A created substitute for God
God's uncreated energies and life
The divine essence as a fourth part
Only information about God
questions.explanation: The energies are uncreated: God's own life, glory, and activity. Participation is real, but it is by grace, not by essence.

questions.prompt: Which statement states the distinction without breaking it?
choices: The energies are a second god beside the essence
Grace is only a created gift and not God's own life
God is unknowable in essence and truly known and shared by His energies
To know God means to comprehend the essence
questions.explanation: That sentence keeps both biblical truths: Exodus guards the essence; Tabor and 2 Peter guard real participation.

challenges.title: Pronounce the Faith I: God and Christ
challenges.summary: Learn to say the big words of the faith out loud — hypostasis, homoousios, Theotokos, communicatio idiomatum — and explain each one in a single clean sentence.
challenges.source: Philippians 2:5-11 · Luke 1:43 · the councils of Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon

lessons.heading: Three words for who God is
lessons.body: Say them slowly first. Ousia (oo-SEE-ah) means essence or being — what God is. Hypostasis (high-PAH-stuh-sis) means the concrete Person — who God is. Physis (FEE-sis) means nature — what a thing is and how it acts. Explain it clean like this: "God is one ousia in three hypostases. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three gods, because they share one divine nature; and they are not one Person wearing masks, because each Person is truly distinct." When a friend says "three Persons means three gods," that sentence is your whole answer.

lessons.heading: One word that guards the Son
lessons.body: Homoousios (hoh-moh-OO-see-ahs) means "of one essence" — the Son is the same in being as the Father, not merely similar to him. Nicaea chose this word in 325 because every softer word left room for the Son to be a creature. Explain it like this: "Jesus is not almost God or partly God. Whatever the Father is as God, the Son is, because they share one essence." The difference between homoousios (same essence) and homoiousios (similar essence) is one small letter — and the whole gospel. The Church fought for the small letter because salvation needs a Savior who is truly God.

lessons.heading: Theotokos, kenosis, communicatio idiomatum
lessons.body: Theotokos (theh-oh-TOH-kohs) means God-bearer: the title for Mary because the child she bore is God the Son in the flesh (Luke 1:43). Kenosis (keh-NOH-sis) means self-emptying, from Philippians 2:7 — the Son emptied himself not by losing divinity but by taking a servant's form. Communicatio idiomatum (kah-myoo-nih-KAH-tee-oh ih-dee-OH-mah-tum) means the exchange of properties: because Christ is one Person in two natures, we can say "God suffered in the flesh" and "the man Jesus is Lord of glory," without mixing the natures. Explain it like this: "Whatever either nature does, the one Person does — so the cross is truly God's own suffering for us, in the flesh."

questions.prompt: What does homoousios confess about the Son?
choices: He is similar in essence to the Father
He is of one essence with the Father — truly God
He is the Father's first creature
questions.explanation: Homoousios means of one essence: the Son is what the Father is as God, not a similar being and not a creature.

questions.prompt: A friend says, "Three Persons means three gods." What is the cleanest first reply?
choices: "The Persons are three separate beings who cooperate"
"One God: Father, Son, and Spirit are distinct Persons sharing one divine nature"
"The word Trinity is not in the Bible, so it does not matter"
questions.explanation: One ousia, three hypostases: distinct Persons, one divine nature — not three gods, and not one Person in disguise.

questions.prompt: Why do we call Mary Theotokos (God-bearer)?
choices: Because she is the source of Christ's divinity
Because the child she bore is God the Son in the flesh — the title guards who Jesus is
Because the Church honors her above God
questions.explanation: Theotokos is a Christological title: it confesses that the one born of Mary is God the Son himself (Luke 1:43; Ephesus, 431).

questions.prompt: What does communicatio idiomatum let us say truthfully?
choices: That the divine nature suffered by itself, apart from the flesh
That the one Person of Christ both was born of Mary and is eternal God, because the properties of both natures belong to the one Person
That the two natures merged into one mixed nature
questions.explanation: The exchange of properties follows from one Person in two unconfused natures: born of Mary according to the flesh, eternal according to divinity.

challenges.title: Pronounce the Faith II: Grace and the inner life
challenges.summary: Perichoresis, theosis, synergeia, logismoi, krasis, the gnomic will — say the words of the Christian life out loud and learn to explain each one plainly.
challenges.source: 2 Peter 1:4 · John 17:21-23 · St. Maximus the Confessor · St. John of Damascus

lessons.heading: Perichoresis and theosis
lessons.body: Perichoresis (peh-ree-koh-REE-sis) means mutual indwelling: the Father, Son, and Spirit dwell in one another without confusion, and Christ prays that we would be drawn into that same communion (John 17:21). Theosis (theh-OH-sis) means deification: by grace we become "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4) — not God by essence, but truly united to God by his uncreated energies. Explain it like this: "God does not only forgive us from far away. He gives us his own life, the way fire makes iron glow: the iron stays iron, but it burns with the fire's heat."

lessons.heading: Synergeia: God does not save us without us
lessons.body: Synergeia (sin-EHR-gee-ah) means synergy, working-together. Salvation is neither God dragging a puppet nor man climbing alone. The classic line runs: "He who created you without you will not save you without you" (St. Augustine). Grace heals and elevates the will; it never coerces it. Explain it with your hands: "God opens the door and gives me the strength to walk — but the walking is really mine. He treats me as a person, not a stone." A stone is moved wholly from outside; a son is moved by love from inside, and his yes is genuinely his own.

lessons.heading: Logismoi, krasis, and the gnomic will
lessons.body: Logismoi (loh-geez-MEE) are the assaultive thoughts or urges — Evagrius listed eight that take turns pressing on the soul: gluttony, lust, greed, sadness, anger, acedia (listless despair), vainglory, pride. Krasis (KRAH-sis) is the mixture or temperament of body and soul; Nemesius of Emesa taught that different mixtures incline different people toward different ruling passions. Thelema gnomikon (THEH-leh-mah noh-MEE-kon) is the gnomic will, St. Maximus's term for our personal, deliberating way of choosing, shaped by temperament and history. Explain it like this: "The fall is one wound, but it bleeds differently in each person. The Fathers diagnose your ruling passion before they prescribe your cure."

questions.prompt: What does theosis mean?
choices: Becoming God by essence, equal to the Father
Partaking of the divine nature by grace — united to God without ceasing to be human
Escaping the body to become pure spirit
questions.explanation: Theosis is participation by grace (2 Peter 1:4): real union with God, while the Creator-creature distinction stands forever.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best explains synergeia (synergy)?
choices: God saves us entirely without our involvement, like moving a stone
We save ourselves; God only watches
Grace heals and strengthens the will, and our free yes is genuinely ours — God does not save us without us
questions.explanation: Synergy: grace never coerces, and man never climbs alone. God gives the healing and the strength; the person truly walks.

questions.prompt: What are the logismoi?
choices: The eight deadly sins everyone commits equally
Assaultive urges (gluttony, lust, greed, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory, pride) that press differently on different souls
The eight beatitudes read backwards
questions.explanation: Evagrius's eight logismoi are urges that take turns ruling different souls — which is why the Philokalia diagnoses the ruling passion first.

questions.prompt: What does krasis (temperament) explain, in Nemesius's teaching?
choices: Why the fall expresses itself through different dominant passions in different people
Why some nations are saved and others are not
Why the body is evil and must be escaped
questions.explanation: Krasis is the body-soul mixture: one fallen condition, many dispositions — so the same wound bleeds differently in each person.

challenges.title: Freedom with a dominant difference
challenges.summary: You are free to act on your strongest motive, but you do not choose the will itself: the will follows what the intellect presents as best. Liberty of spontaneity, not liberty of indifference — with ancestral sin, prevenient grace, and synergy held together.
challenges.source: Romans 7:15-25 · John 8:34-36 · Galatians 5:17 · St. Maximus the Confessor · St. Augustine, anti-Pelagian writings

lessons.heading: Spontaneity, not indifference
lessons.body: Here is the claim in one breath: you always act on your strongest motive at the moment of action. You are free — nothing outside you forces your hand — but you do not stand above your own will picking it like a tool. The will follows what the intellect presents as best, here, now, under the light you actually have. This is liberty of spontaneity: the freedom of a living thing acting from its own nature and loves. Liberty of indifference — a will balanced on nothing, choosing for no reason — would not be freedom at all; a choice with no motive behind it would be random, and randomness is not yours. The dominant difference, the motive that outweighs the rest, is where every real choice is decided.

lessons.heading: Ancestral sin: wounded, not destroyed
lessons.body: The fall, in the Church's teaching, is ancestral sin: what we inherit is mortality and corruption, not personal guilt for Adam's act and not a will smashed to pieces. The will is wounded and bent — it has a dominant bent toward sin — and St. Augustine's later anti-Pelagian writings insist the wounded will cannot will the good without prevenient grace, grace that goes before and heals. But healing is not replacement. Grace elevates the will the way light heals an eye: the eye still sees; it just finally can. That is synergy — God does not save us without us — because a coerced yes would not be love, and love is the whole point.

lessons.heading: Why sin pulls different people different ways
lessons.body: The fall is one, but its wounds show up differently in each person. Nemesius of Emesa (On the Nature of Man) teaches that the soul's movements follow the body's temperament (krasis): different mixtures produce different dispositions, so the same fallen condition expresses itself through different dominant passions. Evagrius's eight logismoi are not eight sins everyone commits equally; they are eight urges that take turns ruling different souls — which is why the Philokalia's whole method is diagnostic first: discern your ruling passion before prescribing the cure. St. Maximus adds the personal depth: the gnomic will (thelema gnomikon) is each person's own mode of deliberating, shaped by disposition and history. No two are alike, so no two cures are alike.

questions.prompt: What is liberty of spontaneity?
choices: Choosing with no motive at all, balanced between options
Acting freely from your own strongest motive — the will follows what the intellect presents as best
Being forced by your strongest desire against your will
questions.explanation: Spontaneity: you act on the dominant motive without external coercion. Indifference — motiveless choice — would be randomness, not freedom.

questions.prompt: In the doctrine of ancestral sin, what do we inherit from Adam?
choices: Personal guilt for Adam's sin and a totally destroyed will
Mortality and corruption; the will is wounded and bent, not destroyed
Nothing at all — each person starts perfectly neutral
questions.explanation: Ancestral sin passes on mortality and corruption. The will is wounded with a dominant bent toward sin — real damage, not annihilation.

questions.prompt: Why can the wounded will not simply will the good on its own?
choices: Because God refuses to help until we perform
Because its dominant bent is toward sin; it needs prevenient grace to heal and elevate it — without coercion
Because the intellect is too weak to know anything
questions.explanation: Augustine's anti-Pelagian point: grace goes before (prevenient), heals the bent will, and the healed will truly chooses — grace elevates, never overrides.

questions.prompt: Why do different people struggle with different ruling sins?
choices: Because God assigns each person a different test at random
Because temperament (krasis) and personal history shape each gnomic will differently, so the one fall expresses itself through different dominant passions
Because some people are simply born worse than others
questions.explanation: Nemesius on temperament, Evagrius on the logismoi, Maximus on the gnomic will: one wound, different dispositions — diagnosis before cure.

challenges.title: Ladder 1 · The Union Itself
challenges.summary: Ladder session 1 of 6. One Person, two natures: hypostatic union, enhypostasia, the Logos before and in the flesh, kenosis, and the Chalcedonian definition.
challenges.source: John 1:1-14 · Philippians 2:5-11 · the Definition of Chalcedon (451)

lessons.heading: One Person, two natures
lessons.body: Start with the two questions every Christology term answers. Hypostasis (high-PAH-stuh-sis) answers who: the concrete subject, the one who acts and speaks. Physis (FEE-sis), nature, answers what: the kind of being, with its powers and limits. In Christ there is one who — God the Word, the second hypostasis of the Trinity — and two whats: the full divine nature and a complete human nature, body and rational soul. This is the hypostatic union: the natures are united not in a mixture and not side by side, but in the one Person of the Word. Say it clean: "One and the same Christ: true God and true man, one Person in two natures."

lessons.heading: Enhypostasia: whose person is the human nature?
lessons.body: Ask the sharp question: Jesus' human nature — does it have its own human person? Enhypostasia (en-hee-pah-STAH-see-ah) answers: the human nature is real and complete, but it has no hypostasis of its own; it exists in the hypostasis of the Word. Enhypostasia names that positive fact. Anhypostasia (an-hee-pah-STAH-see-ah) is its shadow side, and it cuts two ways: rightly used, it says the human nature never existed as a separate person (anhypostatic in itself); wrongly imagined, it would mean a human person of its own — and that is the doorway to Nestorianism. St. Leontius and St. Maximus hold both together: not its own person (anhypostasia), yet not floating loose — personally grounded in the Word (enhypostasia).

lessons.heading: The Word before the flesh, and in the flesh
lessons.body: Logos (LOH-gohs) is the Word, the second Person of the Trinity, eternally begotten of the Father. The Fathers distinguish the Logos asarkos (ah-SAHR-kohs), the Word before the flesh — the eternal Son as he is without our nature — from the Logos ensarkos (en-SAHR-kohs), the same Word enfleshed, after he took flesh from the Virgin. One and the same subject in both names: the one who is eternal is the one who is born. This taking is the incarnation (in-kar-NAY-shun), and the manner of it is called the assumption: the Word assumed, took into himself, a human nature — he did not meet a ready-made man and move in. Theotokos (theh-oh-TOH-kohs), God-bearer, is Mary's title because the one she bore according to the flesh is personally God the Word.

lessons.heading: Kenosis and the Chalcedonian fence
lessons.body: Kenosis (keh-NOH-sis) is the self-emptying of Philippians 2:7: the Son emptied himself "taking the form of a servant" — not by shedding divinity, which is impossible, but by adding humility, veiling glory under flesh that could hunger, suffer, and die. Against every shortcut, the Council of Chalcedon (451) set four fences around the mystery: the two natures are united without confusion (against mixing), without change (the divine nature is not converted into flesh), without division (against splitting Christ into two sons), and without separation (the union never comes apart, not even in death). One Person, two natures, four fences: that is the Chalcedonian definition, and everything in this ladder hangs on it.

questions.prompt: What does hypostasis name, as distinct from physis (nature)?
choices: The who: the concrete Person who acts; nature names the what
The what; nature names the who
A third thing between person and nature
The appearance a nature shows to others
questions.explanation: Hypostasis = the subject, the who (God the Word). Physis = the what, the kind of being. Christ: one who, two whats.

questions.prompt: What is the hypostatic union?
choices: Two natures blended into one new nature
Two persons cooperating closely

challenges.title: Ladder 2 · The Properties
challenges.summary: Ladder session 2 of 6. Idioms of each nature, the communicatio idiomatum, and why we name the Person concretely but never predicate abstractly of a nature.
challenges.source: 1 Corinthians 2:8 · Acts 20:28 · St. Cyril of Alexandria, Third Letter to Nestorius

lessons.heading: Idioms: what belongs to each nature
lessons.body: An idiom (IH-dee-um) is a distinctive attribute, a property proper to one nature. The divine idioms: eternal, uncreated, omnipotent, omnipresent, impassible (unable to suffer in the divine nature itself). The human idioms: born, hungry, weary, crucified, died. Keep the two lists clean in your mind, because the whole art of speaking about Christ is knowing which list a word belongs to — and then daring to say it of the one Person anyway. Scripture does this constantly: "they crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8); the church of God "purchased with his own blood" (Acts 20:28). Born and died are human idioms; Lord of glory and God are divine names; the sentences are true because the subject is one.

lessons.heading: The rule: communicatio idiomatum
lessons.body: Communicatio idiomatum (kah-myoo-nih-KAH-tee-oh ih-dee-OH-mah-tum) means the exchange or sharing of properties, and it is a rule of speech that follows from the hypostatic union. Because the two natures are united in one Person, the idioms of either nature may be predicated of the Person. So we say, without blinking: God was born of a virgin (according to the flesh). The man Jesus is eternal (according to divinity). God suffered and died (according to the human nature he made his own). The rule does not mix the natures — the divinity does not become passible, the flesh does not become uncreated. It assigns every predicate to the one subject, and lets the natures keep their own properties untouched.

lessons.heading: Concrete names yes, abstract names no
lessons.body: Here is the precision tool, taught by the Fathers and sharpened by St. John of Damascus. Concrete predication names the Person by either nature, and it is always allowed: "God" and "man" are concrete terms, so "God died" and "this man is uncreated" can both be confessed — of the one Christ, each according to the other nature. Abstract predication names a nature itself — "the divinity," "the humanity" — and here we refuse the exchange: we never say "the divinity died" or "the humanity is uncreated," because the natures as such do not trade properties. When a debate gets tangled, ask one question: are we naming the Person, or a nature? That single distinction unties most knots.

questions.explanation: Properties of the divine nature: eternal, uncreated, omnipotent, omnipresent, impassible in itself.

questions.prompt: Why can Scripture say "they crucified the Lord of glory"?
choices: Because the divine nature suffered by itself
Because the one Person crucified in the flesh is the Lord of glory — idioms are predicated of the Person
Because glory is a created quality
It is poetry and not meant to be true
questions.explanation: Concrete predication: the subject is God the Word; crucifixion is his according to the flesh he made his own.

questions.prompt: The communicatio idiomatum does NOT mean...
choices: That both natures' idioms can be said of the one Person
That the natures exchange or trade their properties with each other
That "God suffered in the flesh" is true speech
That Acts 20:28 can speak of God's own blood
questions.explanation: The natures never swap properties — divinity stays impassible, flesh stays created. The Person receives both sets of predicates.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses abstract predication wrongly?
choices: "God was born of the Virgin, according to the flesh"
"The divinity died on the cross"
"This man is the eternal Word"
"The Lord of glory was crucified"
questions.explanation: "The divinity" names the nature in the abstract; natures do not die. The Person died, according to his human nature.

questions.prompt: What question unties most tangled Christology arguments?
choices: "Who wrote this first?"
"Are we naming the Person, or a nature?"
"Which council was latest?"
"Is this word Greek or Latin?"
questions.explanation: Concrete terms (God, man, Christ, the Word) take both idioms; abstract terms (divinity, humanity) never trade them.

questions.prompt: The human idioms — born, hungry, crucified, died — belong to Christ...
choices: Only in appearance
According to his human nature, and are truly said of God the Word
Only before the resurrection
As metaphors for spiritual states
questions.explanation: Really his, according to the flesh — and because the flesh is the Word's own, truly predicated of God the Son.

challenges.title: Deep Dive · Communicatio Idiomatum
challenges.summary: The sharing of properties, in full: because the natures are united in one Person, what belongs to either nature can be said of that one Person — while the properties themselves never leave their natures.
challenges.source: 1 Corinthians 2:8 · Acts 20:28 · St. Cyril of Alexandria · St. John of Damascus, On the Orthodox Faith III

lessons.heading: The rule
lessons.body: Communicatio idiomatum (kah-myoo-nih-KAH-tee-oh ih-dee-OH-mah-tum) is Latin for the sharing of properties, and the rule is one sentence: because the divine and human natures are united in one Person, what belongs to either nature can be said of that one Person. The union is in the hypostasis, so predication follows the hypostasis. Whoever Jesus is — and he is God the Word — everything true of his divinity and everything true of his humanity is true of him. That is why Scripture speaks with such holy boldness: "they crucified the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8); the church of God was "purchased with his own blood" (Acts 20:28). The sentences are not exaggerations. They are the grammar of the incarnation.

lessons.heading: What is shared — and what is not
lessons.body: Here is where most people slip. What is shared is not the natures, and not the properties between them. The properties stay distinct, each with its own nature: divine idioms like eternal and uncreated; human idioms like born, hungry, and died. Divinity does not become hungry; flesh does not become uncreated. What is shared is the Person: the Son is the one subject of both sets of properties. Keep the formula by heart: properties stay with their natures; the Person carries both. If the properties themselves were shared between the natures, the natures would be mixed — and Chalcedon's first fence, "without confusion," would fall.

lessons.heading: What you can say, and what you cannot
lessons.body: Because the Person carries both, you can say: "God was born of Mary." "The Lord of glory was crucified." "The blood of God." Each names the Person — God, the Lord of glory — and predicates of him what is his according to the flesh. What you cannot say: "Divinity was born." "Humanity created the world." That is abstract predication, naming a nature itself, and it is refused — you never transfer a property from one nature into the other. The test in any sentence is one question: does it name the Person (concrete: God, man, Christ, the Word), or a nature (abstract: divinity, humanity)? Concrete takes both idioms. Abstract takes only its own.

lessons.heading: The key distinction, the two ditches, and the memory hook
lessons.body: Natures don't die. Death is a property of the human nature. The Person dies in his human nature. So when you say "God died," you mean the Person who is God died — not that the divine nature became mortal. Cross the lines and you land in one of two ditches: say the divine nature itself died, and you have mixed the natures — Eutychianism. Say a man died who was separate from God, and you have split the Person — Nestorianism. The rule threads between them. And the memory hook: communicate means sharing; idiom means a distinctive property. The phrase literally means sharing of properties — and the sharing happens at the level of the Person, not the natures.

questions.prompt: State the rule of communicatio idiomatum precisely:
choices: The natures share their properties with each other in the union
Because the natures are united in one Person, what belongs to either nature can be said of that one Person
Divine properties are transferred into the human nature at the incarnation
We may speak of Christ only in terms of his divinity
questions.explanation: Predication follows the hypostasis. The union is personal, so the one subject carries both sets of properties.

questions.prompt: What exactly is shared in the communicatio idiomatum?
choices: The properties, which pass between the natures
The natures, which merge into one
The Person: the Son is the one subject of both sets of properties, while the properties stay with their natures
Only the divine properties, given to the humanity
questions.explanation: Properties stay with their natures; the Person carries both. Sharing happens at the level of the Person, not the natures.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is refused, and why?
choices: "God was born of Mary" — God cannot be born
"The Lord of glory was crucified" — glory cannot suffer
"Divinity was born" — abstract predication names a nature, and properties are never transferred between natures
"The blood of God" — blood is too lowly for God
questions.explanation: "God was born" names the Person and stands. "Divinity was born" names the nature in the abstract and is refused.

questions.prompt: When we say "God died," we mean...
choices: The divine nature became mortal and died
The Person who is God died in his human nature; natures don't die, persons do
A man died while God watched from a distance
Death is an illusion, so nothing really died
questions.explanation: Death is an idiom of the human nature. The subject who undergoes it is God the Word — that is the whole wonder of the confession.

questions.prompt: Saying the divine nature itself died falls into which ditch?
choices: Nestorianism — splitting the Person
Docetism — denying the flesh
Eutychianism — mixing the natures
Adoptionism — promoting a man
questions.explanation: If divinity as divinity dies, the natures have been blended. The other ditch — a separate man dying — is Nestorianism.

questions.prompt: The memory hook: communicatio idiomatum literally means...
choices: The union of two natures into one
Sharing of properties — and the sharing happens at the level of the Person, not the natures
God speaking through a man
The exchange of natures at the incarnation
questions.explanation: Communicate, sharing; idiom, a distinctive property. Properties stay home; the Person carries both.

challenges.title: Deep Dive · Concrete vs. Abstract Predication
challenges.summary: Every statement about Christ has a subject — a Person or a nature — and which one you pick determines whether the statement is true. Concrete predication names the Person and stands; abstract predication names a nature and is refused.
challenges.source: 1 Corinthians 2:8 · John 1:14 · St. John of Damascus, On the Orthodox Faith III

lessons.heading: The rule: find the subject
lessons.body: Every statement about Christ has a subject, and the subject is either a person or a nature. Which one you pick determines whether the statement is true. A nature is what something is — divinity, humanity. A person is who does something — the Son, the Word, Christ. Natures do not act, speak, hunger, or suffer; persons do, according to their natures. So before you judge any sentence about Christ, ask the one question this whole deep dive runs on: who or what is the subject? If the subject is the Person, the sentence may carry the properties of both natures. If the subject is a nature itself, it may carry only its own.

lessons.heading: Concrete predication: the Person is the subject
lessons.body: Concrete predication names the person — God, the Son, the Word, the man Christ Jesus — and it is true even when the predicate comes from the other nature. "The Son of God died." "God was born of Mary." "The Lord of glory was crucified." These are true because the person is the subject, and the one person possesses both natures entire. Death belongs to the human nature, but the one who died is the divine Son. Born belongs to the flesh, but the one born is God the Word. This is the communicatio idiomatum at work in grammar: properties stay with their natures; the person carries both. Refusing to speak this way is not humility — it quietly splits Christ in two.

lessons.heading: Abstract predication: a nature as subject
lessons.body: Abstract predication names a nature itself — divinity, humanity, the divine nature — and here the exchange is refused. "Divinity was born." "Humanity created the world." "The divine nature suffered." These are false, because natures don't act or suffer — only persons do. A nature is what something is, not who does something. The divine nature as such is impassible; it does not become mortal. The human nature as such is created; it does not create the world. The correction is never to soften the claim but to fix the subject: not "divinity suffered," but "God suffered in the flesh"; not "humanity was crucified," but "the Lord of glory was crucified." Same events, true grammar.

lessons.heading: The formula, the two doorways, and practice
lessons.body: The formula carries the whole lesson: properties stay with their natures; the person carries both. You can say the person did what either nature does, but you cannot say the nature itself did it. Watch the two doorways. Abstract predication is the doorway to Eutychianism: say divinity suffered, and you have made the divine nature mortal — the natures are mixed. Refusing concrete predication is the doorway to Nestorianism: if you cannot say God died, you have split Christ into two persons. Now practice. "The Word became flesh" — concrete: the subject is the Word, the Person. "The human nature was crucified" — abstract, refused: say instead, Christ was crucified according to the flesh. "Christ rose from the dead" — concrete: Christ is the Person, and he rose. Sort the subject first, and you will rarely miss.

questions.prompt: What determines whether a statement about Christ is true?
choices: How traditional the wording sounds
Whether the subject is the Person or a nature
Which council used the sentence first
Whether the predicate sounds humble
questions.explanation: Find the subject first. A Person as subject carries both natures' properties; a nature as subject carries only its own.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is concrete predication — and true?
choices: "The divine nature suffered on the cross"
"The Son of God died"
"Humanity created the world"
"Divinity was born of Mary"
questions.explanation: The subject is the Person, the Son of God; death is his according to the human nature he made his own.

questions.prompt: Why is "the divine nature suffered" false?
choices: Because suffering is beneath God's dignity in every sense
Because natures don't act or suffer — only persons do; the Person suffered in the flesh, the nature as such remains impassible
Because the cross was not real suffering
Because "nature" is a Latin word
questions.explanation: A nature is what something is, not who does something. Fix the subject: God suffered — in the flesh.

questions.prompt: Refusing concrete predication — being unable to say "God died" — is the doorway to...
choices: Eutychianism
Docetism
Nestorianism: Christ split into two persons
Apollinarianism
questions.explanation: If God did not die, then someone else did — a man alongside God. Two subjects, two persons: the Nestorian split.

questions.prompt: Abstract predication — "divinity suffered" — is the doorway to...
choices: Nestorianism
Eutychianism: the divine nature made mortal, the natures mixed
Monothelitism
Adoptionism
questions.explanation: Transfer a human property into the divine nature itself and the natures blend. Properties stay with their natures.

questions.prompt: Classify this one: "The human nature was crucified."
choices: Concrete and true
Abstract and refused — say instead: the Lord of glory was crucified, according to the flesh
Concrete but false
Abstract and true
questions.explanation: The subject names a nature. Natures are not crucified; persons are. The Person was crucified in the nature that can be crucified.

challenges.title: Ladder 3 · The Heresies to Avoid
challenges.summary: Ladder session 3 of 6. Seven ways to miss Christ: splitting him in two, mixing him into a third thing, shrinking his humanity, or making him a man promoted. Each error names the truth it endangers.
challenges.source: the councils of Ephesus (431), Chalcedon (451), and Constantinople III (680-681)

lessons.heading: Splitting Christ in two: Nestorianism and Adoptionism
lessons.body: Nestorianism (nes-TOR-ee-un-iz-um), named for Nestorius of Constantinople, protects God's transcendence by dividing the subject: the Word dwells in the man Jesus as in a temple — two persons, a man plus God, joined by will and honor rather than by union. Its tell: resisting Theotokos, preferring "Christ-bearer," so that Mary bore only the man. Adoptionism (uh-DOP-shun-iz-um) runs the same split through time: Jesus was a mere man whom God adopted — at his baptism, say — and promoted to divine sonship. Both keep a man at the center who is not personally God, and both leave us with a mediator who is, at bottom, one of us reaching up, not God come down. Ephesus answered: the one born of Mary is God the Word; sonship is by nature and eternal, not by promotion.

lessons.heading: Mixing him into a third thing: Eutychianism and Monophysitism
lessons.body: Eutychianism (yoo-TIK-ee-un-iz-um), from the archimandrite Eutyches, confessed the union so strongly that the natures blurred: after the union, Christ's humanity is absorbed into divinity like a drop of wine in the sea — one mixed nature, neither truly God's nor ours. Monophysitism (moh-noh-FIZ-ih-tiz-um) is its family name: one nature (mono-physis) after the union. The cost is double: his divinity is changed by mixture, and his humanity is no longer consubstantial with us — so it cannot heal us. Chalcedon's first two fences answer directly: without confusion, without change. The Orthodox confession is sometimes called miaphysite language in St. Cyril — "one incarnate nature of God the Word" — but Cyril means one Person, with the natures unconfused; the difference is whether "one" names the Person or a blended nature.

lessons.heading: Shrinking the humanity: Apollinarianism, Monothelitism, Docetism
lessons.body: Apollinarianism (ah-pah-lih-NAIR-ee-un-iz-um) kept a real body but cut the crown: Apollinaris gave Christ a human body and animal soul, with the Logos replacing the human mind (nous). St. Gregory Nazianzen's axe falls: "What is not assumed is not healed" — a mind not assumed is a mind not saved. Monothelitism (moh-noh-THEL-ih-tiz-um) repeated the cut one level down: one will (mono-thelema) in Christ, as if a human will would compete with God's. Constantinople III (681) answered with two natural wills, the human will freely following the divine — Gethsemane's "not my will" only makes sense if a real human will speaks. Docetism (DOH-seh-tiz-um), the oldest of the seven, denied the flesh itself: Christ only seemed (dokein, to appear) human; the suffering was theater. Against all three: complete humanity, body, mind, and will — assumed, and therefore healed.

questions.prompt: Nestorianism's core error is...
choices: One nature after the union
Two persons: a man plus God, joined by honor rather than union
Christ had no human mind
Christ only appeared human
questions.explanation: Two subjects where there is one. Its tell is refusing Theotokos so that Mary bears only the man.

questions.prompt: Why is Adoptionism a cousin of Nestorianism?
choices: Both deny the Spirit's divinity
Both end with a man who is not personally God — united or promoted, never the Word himself
Both mix the natures
Both were condemned at Nicaea
questions.explanation: Whether by indwelling or by promotion at baptism, Jesus remains a man other than God the Word. Sonship becomes a reward, not his eternal nature.

questions.prompt: Eutychianism endangers salvation because...
choices: It makes Christ too human to save
The humanity is absorbed and changed, so it is no longer truly ours to be healed
It divides Christ into two sons
It denies the resurrection body
questions.explanation: A drop of wine lost in the sea: what is not consubstantial with us cannot heal us, and what is mixed is no longer fully either nature.

questions.prompt: How does Orthodox use of Cyril's "one incarnate nature of God the Word" differ from Monophysitism?
choices: It does not differ at all
"One" names the one Person (the incarnate Word), with the natures unconfused; Monophysitism makes one blended nature
Cyril meant the humanity was unreal
It refers to the Trinity, not Christ
questions.explanation: Same phrase family, different referent: one hypostasis, confessed with unconfused natures — which is why Chalcedon could receive Cyril.

questions.prompt: What does Gregory Nazianzen's "what is not assumed is not healed" destroy?
choices: Docetism only
Apollinarianism: a Christ without a human mind leaves our minds unhealed
Adoptionism
Monothelitism only
questions.explanation: If the Logos replaced the human nous, the very faculty that fell first would be the one thing not saved.

questions.prompt: Monothelitism claimed one will in Christ. Why does Gethsemane refute it?
choices: Jesus never prayed about his will
"Not my will, but thine" shows a real human will, distinct and freely following the divine
The disciples heard only one voice
Wills belong to natures, and Christ has one nature
questions.explanation: Two natural wills (dyotheletism): the human will is real, and its glory is free obedience, not absence. Condemned and settled at Constantinople III, 681.

questions.prompt: Docetism is the claim that...
choices: Christ is two persons
Christ only appeared human; the flesh and suffering were seeming
Christ had one will
Christ was adopted at his baptism
questions.explanation: From dokein, to seem. The oldest error in the list — against it, John insists the Word became flesh, and invites Thomas to touch.

challenges.title: Ladder 4 · The Councils
challenges.summary: Ladder session 4 of 6. Five councils, five sentences to remember: Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381, Ephesus 431, Chalcedon 451, Constantinople III 681 — what each one settled and why.
challenges.source: the acts and definitions of the first five ecumenical councils

lessons.heading: Nicaea 325 and Constantinople 381: the Godhead defended
lessons.body: Nicaea (ny-SEE-ah), 325: Arius taught that the Son was the first and greatest creature — "there was when he was not." The council answered with one surgical word, homoousios (hoh-moh-OO-see-ahs): the Son is of one essence with the Father, begotten not made. If the Son were a creature, no creature could unite creatures to God; the whole gospel stood on one word. Constantinople (kon-stan-tih-NOH-pul), 381, finished the sentence for the Spirit: against those who made the Holy Spirit a servant or force, the council confessed him as Lord and Giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, worshipped and glorified together with Father and Son — God, not a gift God gives. Together these two councils give the Creed its spine: one God, three Persons, each fully God.

lessons.heading: Ephesus 431 and Chalcedon 451: the union defined
lessons.body: Ephesus (EF-eh-sus), 431, faced Nestorius, who would not call Mary Theotokos for fear of making her mother of divinity. St. Cyril's logic prevailed: the title is not about Mary's power but the child's identity — the one born of her is God the Word, so she is God-bearer. One Person, from the first moment of conception. Chalcedon (KAL-seh-dun), 451, then drew the map both errors demanded: against Nestorius, one and the same Christ, one Person and one hypostasis; against Eutyches, in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation, the distinction of the natures in no way abolished by the union. Chalcedon's definition is mostly fences — it tells us where the mystery is not, so that worship can find where he is.

lessons.heading: Constantinople III 681: the last cut answered
lessons.body: Two and a half centuries after Chalcedon, the question narrowed to a point: if Christ has two natures, does he have two wills? Monothelitism said one will, to protect unity. Constantinople III (680–681) saw the trap: will belongs to nature, so one will would mean one nature — Eutyches returning through the back door — and a Christ without a human will could not heal ours. The council confessed two natural wills and two natural operations, indivisibly and without confusion, the human will following and subject not by force but in free obedience to the divine. With that, the ladder of councils is complete: God the Son is who Nicaea said (true God), born of whom Ephesus said (Theotokos), united as Chalcedon said (one Person, two natures), and willing as Constantinople III said (his human will, freely ours and freely surrendered).

Perichoresis
Enhypostasia
questions.explanation: Against Arius: begotten, not made, of one essence with the Father. A creature cannot unite creatures to God.

The divinity of the Holy Spirit, worshipped and glorified with Father and Son
Mary's title

questions.explanation: The Spirit is Lord and Giver of life, proceeding from the Father — God himself, not a force or a servant.

questions.prompt: Ephesus (431) confessed Mary as Theotokos in order to confess what about Christ?
choices: That Mary is the source of divinity
That the one born of her is personally God the Word — one Person from conception
That Christ became God at his baptism
That Mary should receive latreia
questions.explanation: The title guards the child's identity. Nestorius's refusal split Christ into a man born and a God indwelling.

questions.prompt: Chalcedon (451) protected the union with which four adverbs?
choices: Begotten, unbegotten, proceeding, sent

questions.explanation: The four fences: no mixing (Eutyches), no converting, no splitting (Nestorius), no separating — ever.

choices: To give Jesus inner conflict
Because will belongs to nature: one will would mean one nature, and an unassumed human will would be unhealed
To honor the emperor's theology
Because Scripture lists two wills by name
questions.explanation: Dyotheletism: two natural wills, the human freely following the divine — Gethsemane's obedience made dogma.

challenges.summary: Ladder session 5 of 6. Cyril and Nestorius at Ephesus, Eutyches the counterweight, Maximus who paid with his tongue and hand, and John of Damascus who wrote the summary the Church still uses.
challenges.source: St. Cyril's Letters to Nestorius · St. Maximus, Disputation with Pyrrhus · St. John of Damascus, On the Orthodox Faith III

lessons.heading: Cyril against Nestorius: the fight over one word for Mary
lessons.body: Nestorius (nes-TOR-ee-us), patriarch of Constantinople, balked at calling Mary Theotokos: God cannot be born, he reasoned, so Mary bore the man in whom the Word dwelt. St. Cyril of Alexandria (SEER-il) saw the split instantly. If the one born of Mary is not God the Word himself, then Jesus is two subjects — a man inspired, indwelt, honored — and the cross becomes the death of a man near God, not God's own death for us in the flesh. Cyril pressed the communicatio idiomatum relentlessly: because the Person is one, Scripture's bold sentences stand — God born, God crucified in the flesh. His Twelve Anathemas and the Second and Third Letters to Nestorius became Ephesus's yardstick: whoever will not confess the one incarnate Word, and Mary as Theotokos, has already divided Christ.

lessons.heading: Eutyches and Maximus: the opposite ditch, and the confessor
lessons.body: Eutyches (YOO-tih-keez), an elderly Constantinople archimandrite, hated Nestorius so much he fell off the other side: before the union, two natures; after the union, one — with the humanity so swallowed by divinity that Christ was not consubstantial with us. Chalcedon deposed him and confessed the natures unconfused. Two centuries later St. Maximus the Confessor (MAK-sih-mus) fought the subtler sequel, monothelitism. His tools were the ones from session 1: the human nature is enhypostatic in the Word, real in every faculty — mind, will, energy — and precisely therefore healed. When emperor and patriarchs demanded silence, Maximus would not trade Christ's human will for peace; they cut out his tongue and cut off his right hand, and he died in exile in 662. Constantinople III vindicated him nineteen years after his death.

lessons.heading: John of Damascus: the summary that closed the age
lessons.body: St. John of Damascus (duh-MAS-kus), writing in the 8th century from the monastery of St. Sabbas, gathered the whole patristic settlement into On the Orthodox Faith — the first great summary, and still the Church's handbook. Book III gives Christology its classic form: one hypostasis, two natures, two wills and energies, the communicatio idiomatum with its concrete and abstract rules, and the phrase that threads everything: the Word "became flesh" without ceasing to be what he was, and the flesh became the Word's own without ceasing to be ours. When you meet a new Christological claim, the Damascene is the test bench: does it keep Cyril's one Person, Chalcedon's unconfused natures, and Maximus's complete humanity — mind, will, and all? If it fails any one, it is one of the seven ditches with new paint.

questions.prompt: What did Cyril see at stake in the word Theotokos?
choices: Mary's personal honor in the empire
Whether the one born of Mary is God the Word himself, or a man merely indwelt by God
Whether bishops may preach about Mary
The date of the Annunciation feast
questions.explanation: Split the child, and the cross is a man's death near God — not God's own saving death in the flesh. Ephesus agreed with Cyril.

questions.prompt: Nestorius preferred to protect God by...
choices: Denying Christ's humanity
Joining the Word and the man by will and honor rather than by personal union
Making the Spirit a creature
Blaming the council system
questions.explanation: Indwelling instead of incarnation: two subjects in close alliance. That is precisely what hypostatic union denies.

questions.prompt: Eutyches's error, in one line:
choices: Two persons in Christ
After the union, one nature, with the humanity absorbed so Christ is not consubstantial with us
No human mind in Christ
Sonship by adoption
questions.explanation: The anti-Nestorian overcorrection. Chalcedon: the natures remain, unconfused and unchanged, in one Person.

questions.prompt: What did Maximus the Confessor lose for confessing Christ's human will?
choices: His monastery only
His tongue and his right hand, dying in exile — vindicated at Constantinople III
A debate in Alexandria
His books were edited, nothing more
questions.explanation: Mutilated in 662 for refusing to silence the two wills; the council of 681 confessed exactly what he died for.

questions.prompt: Maximus's word for how Christ's human nature personally exists is...
choices: Anhypostasia alone, floating free
Enhypostasia: it exists in the hypostasis of the Word
A second hypostasis beside the Word
A prosopon added at the resurrection
questions.explanation: Not its own person, and not ungrounded: enhypostatic in the Word, complete in mind, will, and energy — and so healed.

questions.prompt: Why does the Church still test claims by John of Damascus's On the Orthodox Faith?
choices: It is the newest book on the subject
It is the classic summary: Cyril's one Person, Chalcedon's unconfused natures, Maximus's complete humanity in one bench-test
It replaced the councils
It explains Christ in Latin categories
questions.explanation: Written after the councils, gathering them. A claim that fails any of the three has fallen into one of the seven ditches.

challenges.title: Ladder 6 · The Orthodox Terms
challenges.summary: Ladder session 6 of 6. The wider Orthodox vocabulary the Christology stands in: Panagia, ousia and energies, the essence-energies distinction, theosis, perichoresis, and prosopon.
challenges.source: 2 Peter 1:4 · John 17:21-23 · St. Gregory Palamas, the Triads

lessons.heading: Panagia, and the map of essence and energies
lessons.body: Panagia (pah-nah-GEE-ah) means All-Holy, the Church's beloved title for Mary — the one whose holiness is wholly gift, as ours is meant to be. Around her, the Damascene and St. Gregory Palamas draw the map this whole ladder stands in. Ousia (oo-SEE-ah), essence, answers what God is: the divine being itself, utterly beyond creaturely comprehension — no one has known, or can know, what God is in himself (Exodus 33:20; 1 Timothy 6:16). The energies (EN-er-jeez) answer what God does: his uncreated operations and gifts — life, light, grace, the glory of Tabor — truly God, truly given. The essence-energies distinction holds both: God is unknowable in essence and genuinely knowable in his energies, as the sun is untouchable in its core and warm on your skin.

lessons.heading: Theosis and perichoresis: where the map leads
lessons.body: Theosis (theh-OH-sis) is the destination: becoming by grace what God is by nature — "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4). Not absorption (the Eutychian ditch in mystical dress) and not moral improvement alone: real participation in the uncreated life, while we remain creatures forever. Perichoresis (peh-ree-koh-REE-sis) names the shape of that life in God himself: the mutual indwelling of the Persons — the Father in the Son, the Son in the Father, the Spirit in both — distinct without distance, one without confusion. The same word serves Christology (the natures interpenetrate in the one Person without mixing) and the Trinity, and it is why salvation is pictured as being drawn into a communion that already exists, not admitted to a crowd: "that they all may be one, as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee" (John 17:21).

lessons.heading: Prosopon: the face of the Person
lessons.body: Prosopon (PROH-soh-pon) is the Greek word for face, and in theology for the person as presented — the one you meet, address, and love. It carries both riches and a warning from the ladder's first rungs: in sloppy hands prosopon shrank toward mask or role (the old Sabellian danger, as if the Persons were faces God wears). The councils therefore anchored it: prosopon is true speech when it means hypostasis — a real, distinct who, not a costume. Say the whole ladder back now: one God, one ousia, three hypostases (never three prosopa as masks); in Christ, one hypostasis and prosopon of the Word, two natures with all their idioms, two wills, and the energies of God given to us for theosis. That is the faith of the sessions — hold it, and you can hear any new claim and know within a sentence which ditch it leans toward.

questions.prompt: Panagia means...
choices: Mother of the Trinity
All-Holy — the beloved title of Mary, whose holiness is wholly gift
Queen above the angels by nature
A name for the Church building
questions.explanation: Panagia, All-Holy: the first fruit of the grace the rest of this session describes.

questions.prompt: The essence-energies distinction confesses...
choices: God is partly knowable in his essence if we try hard
God is unknowable in his essence, and truly knowable in his uncreated energies — both, without division
The energies are created effects, so we never meet God himself
Essence and energies are two gods
questions.explanation: Untouchable core, real warmth: we participate in God himself by his energies, while his essence remains forever beyond creatures.

questions.prompt: What is theosis?
choices: Becoming God by essence
Participation in the divine life by grace — becoming by grace what God is by nature, while remaining creatures
Escaping the body and the world as evil
A reward only for monks
questions.explanation: 2 Peter 1:4: partakers of the divine nature. Union without confusion — Chalcedon's pattern applied to our salvation.

questions.prompt: Perichoresis names...
choices: A council procedure
The mutual indwelling of the divine Persons — and, in Christ, of the natures in the one Person — without confusion
The procession of the Spirit only
A style of Byzantine chant
questions.explanation: Distinct without distance, one without confusion. Salvation is being drawn into that existing communion (John 17:21).

questions.prompt: Why did the councils treat prosopon carefully?
choices: It is a Latin word they distrusted
It can shrink toward mask or role; it is safe only when it means hypostasis, a real distinct who
It refers to the human nature only
It was invented by Nestorius
questions.explanation: Face and person — true when anchored to hypostasis, dangerous when it slides toward three masks of one actor.

questions.prompt: Which sentence recites the whole ladder cleanly?
choices: One God in three masks; Christ a God-filled man; salvation by example
One ousia, three hypostases; in Christ one hypostasis of the Word in two natures, two wills, all idioms predicated of the Person; God known in his energies, and we deified by grace
Two persons, one nature, one will; Mary bore a man; God is unknowable entirely
One nature after the union; the essence is given to us as we cease to be creatures
questions.explanation: That is the six sessions in one breath — Godhead, union, properties, heresies avoided, councils, figures, and terms all held together.
